example.problem: A transversal crosses two parallel railway tracks, creating an 80° angle on the left of the first track (inside). What is the alternate interior angle?
example.solution: Alternate interior angles are equal, so the angle on the right of the second track (inside) is also 80°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alternate angles are on opposite sides and are equal when the lines are parallel.

slides.title: Mumbai Traffic Intersection
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev points to a real intersection: two parallel streets with a diagonal road crossing both. 'Rohan, that diagonal is the transversal. Look at all the angles it makes!'

example.problem: A transversal crosses two parallel roads. The transversal makes a 58° angle with the first road. Identify all 8 angles at both intersections.
example.solution:
At the first intersection:
- Angle 1: 58°
- Angle 2 (adjacent): 180° − 58° = 122°
- Angle 3 (opposite to 1): 58°
- Angle 4 (opposite to 2): 122°

At the second intersection (parallel road):
- Angle 5 (corresponding to 1): 58°
- Angle 6 (corresponding to 2): 122°
- Angle 7 (corresponding to 3): 58°
- Angle 8 (corresponding to 4): 122°

Alternatively, using alternate angles:
- Angles 3 and 6 are alternate interior: both 58°
- Angles 2 and 5 are alternate interior: both 122°

slides.title: Co-Interior (Same-Side Interior) Angles

points.label: What are they
points.text: When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, angles on the same side of the transversal and inside the lines are co-interior angles.

points.label: Key property
points.text: Co-interior angles are supplementary—they add to 180°.

points.label: Visual
points.text: Both angles are 'between' the parallel lines and on the same side of the transversal.

points.label: Proof
points.text: If one co-interior angle is 70°, the other is 180° − 70° = 110°.

example.problem: A transversal crosses two parallel lines. One co-interior angle is 85°. What is the other?
example.solution: Co-interior angles sum to 180°. So 180° − 85° = 95°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Co-interior angles are on the same side, between the parallel lines, and they add to 180°.

slides.title: Rohan Tests His Knowledge
slides.storyContext: Rohan decides to test his new knowledge. He draws his own diagram of a street crossing and marks one angle as 72°. 'Can I find all other angles using what I learned?'

slides.title: Rohan's Complete Angle Diagram
slides.storyContext: Rohan draws two intersecting lines and marks one angle as 72°. Then he adds a parallel line with a transversal. He challenges himself to find all angles.

example.problem: Draw two intersecting lines. One angle is 72°. A third line is parallel to one of them, and a transversal cuts both lines. Find all angles at all intersections.
example.solution:
At the first intersection (original two lines):
- Angle A: 72° (given)
- Angle B (adjacent): 180° − 72° = 108°
- Angle C (opposite A): 72°
- Angle D (opposite B): 108°

At the parallel line (transversal with parallel line):
If the transversal makes 72° with the first line,
- Angle E (corresponding): 72°
- Angle F (adjacent): 108°
- Angle G (opposite E): 72°
- Angle H (opposite F): 108°

All angles at both intersections are either 72° or 108°.

slides.title: Real-World Application
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev says: 'In Mumbai, we have many parallel streets. If I know one angle at a street crossing, I can predict angles at every parallel street. That's geometry, beta!'

example.problem: Three parallel streets run north-south. Two transversals cross all three. The first transversal makes a 55° angle with the first street. What angles does it make with the other two streets? What about the second transversal if it makes 55° with the first street?
example.solution:
For the first transversal:
- Street 1: 55° (given) and 125° (supplementary)
- Street 2: 55° (corresponding) and 125° (supplementary)
- Street 3: 55° (corresponding) and 125° (supplementary)

For the second transversal:
- Street 1: 55° and 125°
- Street 2: 55° and 125°
- Street 3: 55° and 125°

Key insight: When a transversal crosses multiple parallel lines, it makes the same angles at every intersection.

slides.title: Rohan Discovers Angle Sum
slides.storyContext: While drawing more diagrams, Rohan notices: 'Wait, if I add up all four angles at an intersection, I always get 360°!' Let's explore this discovery.

slides.title: Angle Sum Around a Point

points.label: Full rotation
points.text: All angles around one point add up to 360° (a complete rotation).

points.label: At an intersection
points.text: Two intersecting lines create 4 angles: a° + b° + c° + d° = 360°.

points.label: Proof using known pairs
points.text: Opposite angles are equal (a=c, b=d). So a + b + a + b = 360, meaning 2a + 2b = 360, thus a + b = 180 (adjacent angles).

points.label: Straight line
points.text: A straight angle is exactly 180° (half the full rotation).

example.problem: Two intersecting lines form angles: 45°, x, 45°, x. Find x.
example.solution:
45 + x + 45 + x = 360
90 + 2x = 360
2x = 270
x = 135°

The angles are 45°, 135°, 45°, 135° (opposite angles are equal).

slides.inSimpleWords: All angles around a point sum to 360°—a complete circle.

slides.title: Reflex Angles

points.text: A reflex angle is between 180 and 360 degrees.
If regular angle is 60, reflex is 360 - 60 = 300.
Reflex angles rare in school but appear in 3D.
Example: spinning wheel can rotate short way or long way.

slides.inSimpleWords: Reflex angle is the long way around the circle.

slides.title: Rohan Draws a Complex Map
slides.storyContext: Rohan marks 3 parallel streets (NS) and 2 transversals crossing them.

slides.title: Angles with Multiple Transversals

points.text: Two transversals crossing parallel lines create patterns.
Each transversal creates same pattern at every parallel line.
Transversal A at 45 degrees: 45, 135, 45, 135 at each line.
Transversal B at 60 degrees: 60, 120, 60, 120 at each line.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each transversal is independent, but follows same rules.

slides.title: Rohan Mumbai Map
slides.storyContext: Transversal A at 48 degrees, Transversal B at 62 degrees.

example.problem: List angles for both at first parallel street

slides.title: Perpendicular Lines

points.text: Two lines are perpendicular if they form 90 degree angle.
Symbol shows right angle.
At intersection: all four angles are 90 degrees.
Real-world: N-S streets perpendicular to E-W streets.

slides.inSimpleWords: Perpendicular means at right angles, like a plus sign.

slides.title: Perpendicular Transversal
slides.storyContext: What if a transversal crosses parallel streets at 90 degrees?

example.problem: Transversal perpendicular to two parallel lines. List all angles.
example.solution: All angles: 90, 90, 90, 90 at every intersection

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Intersecting lines meet at a point and form four angles.
Vertically opposite angles are equal.
Adjacent angles are supplementary (sum to 180°).
A transversal is a line crossing two other lines.
When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal.
Alternate interior angles are equal (on opposite sides, inside parallel lines).
Co-interior angles sum to 180° (on same side, inside parallel lines).
Angles can be acute (sharp), right (90°), obtuse (wide), or straight (180°).
All angles around one point sum to 360°.
Real-world applications include street intersections, railway crossings, and architecture.

slides.inSimpleWords: Road crossings show us that angles follow rules: opposite angles match, and parallel lines with a crossing create matching angles.

subject: Mathematics
title: The Congruent Puzzle
hook: Isha collects passport-sized photos of her friends and notices some are exactly the same size and shape—even when flipped or rotated.

slides.title: The Congruent Puzzle
slides.storyContext: Isha arranges her photo album and notices twin shapes — exact copies in every way.

slides.title: The Discovery
slides.storyContext: Isha is organizing photos for a school project. She finds two photos of the same size and shape. She overlays them — perfect match! Then she finds two photo frames: one is blue, one is red, but they are the exact same shape and size. 'These are twins!' she exclaims. Akshay joins her: 'In geometry, we call them congruent. Let me show you the rules.'
slides.inSimpleWords: When two shapes are exactly the same size and shape, they are congruent — like identical twins.

slides.title: What is Congruence?

points.text: Two figures are congruent if they have the same size and shape.
Congruent figures can be rotated, reflected, or translated (moved), but their dimensions stay the same.
If you cut out both shapes from paper, they would fit perfectly over each other.

example.problem: Are these two triangles congruent? Triangle 1 has sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm. Triangle 2 has sides 5 cm, 3 cm, 4 cm.
example.solution: Yes. Both triangles have the same three side lengths (3, 4, 5), just listed in different order. They are congruent.

slides.inSimpleWords: Congruent shapes are identical copies — same size, same shape, no tricks.

slides.title: Isha's Photo Album Adventure
slides.storyContext: Isha pulls out a stack of old photos. Some are 4×6 cm, and some are also 4×6 cm but rotated. 'Look, Akshay! Same size, but this one is standing up and this one is sideways.' Akshay nods: 'Both are congruent. Rotation doesn't change congruence — the shape and size stay identical.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Rotating a shape does not destroy congruence — it remains identical to the original.

slides.title: Congruent Triangles

points.text: Two triangles are congruent if all three sides of one match all three sides of the other (SSS rule).
Or: if two sides and the included angle match (SAS rule).
Or: if two angles and a side match in the right way (ASA or AAS rule).

example.problem: Triangle ABC has sides AB = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm, CA = 7 cm. Triangle PQR has sides PQ = 5 cm, QR = 6 cm, RP = 7 cm. Are they congruent?
example.solution: Yes, by SSS (Side-Side-Side). All three sides match.

slides.inSimpleWords: To prove two triangles are congruent, check that their sides or sides-and-angles match.

slides.title: SSS Rule in Action
slides.storyContext: Isha cuts out two triangles from cardstock. Triangle 1: sides 5 cm, 6 cm, 7 cm. Triangle 2: sides 5 cm, 6 cm, 7 cm. She overlays them and they match perfectly.

example.problem: Prove Triangle 1 and Triangle 2 are congruent using SSS.
example.solution: All three sides are equal: 5 cm = 5 cm, 6 cm = 6 cm, 7 cm = 7 cm. By SSS, the triangles are congruent.

slides.inSimpleWords: SSS means all three sides match — if that's true, the triangles are congruent.

slides.title: SAS Rule (Side-Angle-Side)

points.text: Two triangles are congruent if two sides and the angle between them (the included angle) match.
The angle MUST be between the two sides for the rule to work.
Example: Side 5 cm, Angle 60°, Side 6 cm matches the other triangle's Side 5 cm, Angle 60°, Side 6 cm.

example.problem: Triangle A: sides 4 cm, 5 cm with a 45° angle between them. Triangle B: sides 4 cm, 5 cm with a 45° angle between them. Congruent?
example.solution: Yes, by SAS. Two sides and the included angle are equal.

slides.inSimpleWords: SAS: if two sides and the angle between them match, the triangles are congruent.

slides.title: Akshay's Angle Challenge
slides.storyContext: Akshay draws two triangles. 'Isha, look at this. Triangle 1 has two sides of 6 cm and 8 cm with a 50° angle between them. Triangle 2 also has 6 cm and 8 cm with 50° between them. Are they congruent?' Isha thinks and says: 'Yes! The included angle is the same, so by SAS, they are congruent.'
slides.inSimpleWords: SAS is powerful — knowing two sides and their angle is enough to prove congruence.

slides.title: ASA Rule (Angle-Side-Angle)

points.text: Two triangles are congruent if two angles and the side between them (included side) match.
The side MUST be between the two angles.
If Angle 1 = Angle 1', Side = Side', Angle 2 = Angle 2', then triangles are congruent.

example.problem: Triangle C: Angle 50°, Side 7 cm, Angle 60°. Triangle D: Angle 50°, Side 7 cm, Angle 60°. Congruent?
example.solution: Yes, by ASA. Two angles and the included side are equal.

slides.inSimpleWords: ASA: two angles and the side between them — that's congruence.

slides.title: Akshay's SSS Challenge
slides.storyContext: Akshay asks Isha: 'If I tell you a triangle has three sides of 5, 6, and 7 cm, can you draw another triangle that's NOT congruent to it?' Isha thinks: 'No! If all three sides are the same, the triangle must be congruent to the original. That's the SSS rule!'
slides.inSimpleWords: The SSS rule guarantees congruence — you cannot build a different triangle with the same three side lengths.

slides.title: Comparing Different Triangle Rules
slides.storyContext: Isha learns the triangle rules: SSS (all sides), SAS (two sides + angle), ASA (two angles + side), AAS (two angles + non-included side). Akshay says: 'Each rule is a shortcut — you don't need to check everything, just these key measurements.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Triangle congruence rules are shortcuts — knowing specific measurements is enough.

slides.title: Which Rule Applies?
slides.storyContext: Isha has Triangle P: sides 4, 5, 6. Triangle Q: angle 30°, side 4, angle 50°. Can she prove they're congruent? No—she has different information.

example.problem: To prove Triangle P ≅ Triangle Q, what info would you need?
example.solution: You'd need matching side lengths OR matching angles with a side. Different types of info cannot be mixed across triangles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the right rule for the information you have.

slides.title: AAS Rule (Angle-Angle-Side)
slides.storyContext: Akshay draws AAS: Angle 40°, Angle 70°, and a non-included Side 8 cm. He draws the same for another triangle. 'Both triangles have the same two angles and a side NOT between them. Are they congruent?' Yes — AAS guarantees it.

example.problem: Triangle R: Angle 40°, Angle 70°, Side 8 cm (not between angles). Triangle S: Angle 40°, Angle 70°, Side 8 cm (not between angles). Congruent?
example.solution: Yes, by AAS. Two angles and a non-included side match.

slides.inSimpleWords: AAS is like ASA but the side is NOT between the angles.

slides.title: Congruent Polygons

points.text: For any polygon (triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon, etc.) to be congruent, all sides must be equal and all angles must be equal.
Two squares with the same side length are always congruent.
Two rectangles with the same length and width are congruent.

example.problem: Square A has a side of 4 cm. Square B has a side of 4 cm. Square C has a side of 5 cm. Which squares are congruent?
example.solution: Squares A and B are congruent (both have 4 cm sides). Square C is not congruent to A or B.

slides.inSimpleWords: Polygons with matching sides and angles are twins in geometry.

image.alt: Congruent Polygons — Geometric Twins

slides.title: Rectangle Congruence
slides.storyContext: Isha finds two rectangular photo frames. Frame 1: 20 cm long, 15 cm wide. Frame 2: 20 cm long, 15 cm wide.

example.problem: Are the frames congruent?
example.solution: Yes. Both have matching length (20 cm) and width (15 cm). All angles in both are 90°, so they are congruent.

slides.inSimpleWords: Two rectangles with the same length and width are congruent — all angles are 90° anyway.

slides.title: Reflection and Congruence

points.text: When you flip a shape over a line (called reflection), the new shape is congruent to the original.
The original and reflected shapes are mirror images.
All measurements stay the same; only position and orientation change.

example.problem: Isha reflects a triangle over a vertical line. Is the reflected triangle congruent to the original?
example.solution: Yes. Reflection preserves size and shape, so congruence is maintained.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mirrors create congruent twins — a reflection of a shape is the same shape, just flipped.

slides.title: The Mirror Trick
slides.storyContext: Isha places a triangle against a mirror and sees its reflection. 'Akshay, the reflected triangle looks different, but is it the same?' Akshay replies: 'Measure it. The reflected triangle is congruent — same size and shape, just flipped like a mirror image.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Reflections preserve congruence — the mirror image is congruent to the original.

slides.title: Rotation and Congruence

points.text: When you rotate a shape around a point, the new shape is congruent to the original.
You can rotate by any amount (90°, 180°, 270°, etc.), and congruence is still true.
Only position and orientation change; size and shape stay the same.

example.problem: A square is rotated 45° around its center. Is it congruent to the original square?
example.solution: Yes. Rotation preserves size and shape, so congruence is maintained.

slides.inSimpleWords: Spin a shape, and it remains congruent to itself — just tilted differently.

image.alt: Rotation and Congruence — Geometric Twins

slides.title: Rotation in Action
slides.storyContext: Isha rotates a star shape 90° clockwise. The star looks tilted now, but is it congruent?

example.problem: A star is rotated 90° clockwise. Are the original and rotated stars congruent?
example.solution: Yes. Rotation preserves size and shape. The rotated star is congruent to the original.

slides.inSimpleWords: No matter how much you rotate a shape, it remains congruent to itself.

slides.title: Translation and Congruence

points.text: Translation means moving a shape from one place to another without rotating or flipping it.
A translated shape is always congruent to the original.
Moving a triangle 5 cm to the right keeps it congruent.

example.problem: A triangle is moved 10 cm to the left. Is it congruent to the original?
example.solution: Yes. Translation preserves size and shape, so the moved triangle is congruent to the original.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sliding a shape (translation) does not change congruence — it stays identical.

slides.title: Isha's Photo Frame Problem
slides.storyContext: Isha has a rectangular photo frame that is 20 cm long and 15 cm wide. She buys another frame and measures it: 15 cm long and 20 cm wide. Are the frames congruent?

example.problem: Frame 1: length 20 cm, width 15 cm. Frame 2: length 15 cm, width 20 cm. Are they congruent?
example.solution: If Frame 2 is rotated 90°, its dimensions match Frame 1 (both 20×15). Yes, they are congruent.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes are congruent even if one is rotated — just check if rotating makes them match.

slides.title: Isha Tests Her Friends
slides.storyContext: Isha shows her friends two quadrilaterals. Quadrilateral A: sides 5 cm, 6 cm, 5 cm, 6 cm, all angles 90°. Quadrilateral B: rotated 180°, sides 5 cm, 6 cm, 5 cm, 6 cm, all angles 90°. 'Are these congruent?' asks Isha. Her friends check: 'Yes! Rotation doesn't matter if the sides and angles match.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Transformations like rotation, reflection, and translation do not destroy congruence.

slides.title: Identifying Congruent Figures with Transformations
slides.storyContext: Isha draws a pentagon and applies multiple transformations: first rotating it 90°, then translating it 10 cm to the right. 'Is this shape still congruent to the original?' Akshay confirms: 'Yes! All transformations preserve congruence.'

example.problem: A shape undergoes rotation (90°), then translation (5 cm right). Is the final shape congruent to the original?
example.solution: Yes. Each transformation individually preserves congruence, so multiple transformations also preserve congruence.

slides.inSimpleWords: Chain transformations together — congruence is preserved through all of them.

slides.title: Identifying Congruent Figures

points.text: Step 1: Compare all side lengths.
Step 2: Compare all angles.
Step 3: If all sides and all angles match, the figures are congruent.
Transformations (rotation, reflection, translation) do not affect congruence.

example.problem: Figure A: triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 and angles 30°, 60°, 90°. Figure B: triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 and angles 30°, 60°, 90°. Congruent?
example.solution: Yes. All sides match and all angles match. The figures are congruent.

slides.inSimpleWords: To check congruence: match sides, match angles, done!

slides.title: Corresponding Parts of Congruent Figures

points.text: When two figures are congruent, their corresponding sides are equal.
Corresponding angles are also equal.
Example: If Triangle ABC ≅ Triangle DEF, then AB = DE, BC = EF, CA = FD, and angles A = D, B = E, C = F.

example.problem: Triangle ABC ≅ Triangle XYZ. If AB = 5 cm, BC = 7 cm, and angle B = 60°, what are XY, YZ, and angle Y?
example.solution: XY = 5 cm, YZ = 7 cm, angle Y = 60°. Corresponding parts are equal.

slides.inSimpleWords: In congruent shapes, corresponding sides and angles match perfectly.

slides.title: Can You Solve This?
slides.storyContext: Akshay draws two triangles on paper. Triangle 1 has sides 6 cm, 8 cm, and an included angle of 50°. Triangle 2 has sides 6 cm, 8 cm, and the angle between those sides is also 50°. Are they congruent? Then he reflects Triangle 1 over a line. Is the reflection congruent to Triangle 2?

example.problem: Two triangles with SAS (6 cm, 50°, 8 cm) are congruent. If one is reflected, is it still congruent to the other?
example.solution: Yes, both original triangles are congruent (by SAS). After reflection, the reflected triangle is still congruent to both originals.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the rules (SSS, SAS, ASA) to prove congruence, and remember reflections keep congruence.

image.alt: Can You Solve This? — Geometric Twins

slides.title: Advanced Challenge
slides.storyContext: Isha has Triangle ABC with sides AB = 7 cm, BC = 9 cm, CA = 5 cm. She also has Triangle DEF. After measuring, she finds DE = 7 cm, EF = 9 cm, FD = 5 cm. She then rotates Triangle DEF 180° and reflects it. Is the transformed Triangle DEF congruent to Triangle ABC?

example.problem: Two triangles have matching side lengths. After transformation (rotation + reflection), are they still congruent to each other?
example.solution: Yes. Original triangles are congruent by SSS. Rotation and reflection preserve congruence, so the transformed triangle is still congruent to Triangle ABC.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiple transformations stacked together still preserve congruence.

slides.title: Congruence Proof Challenge
slides.storyContext: Isha receives a complex challenge: Given quadrilateral PQRS with sides 4 cm, 5 cm, 6 cm, 7 cm and angles 80°, 100°, 90°, 90°. Given quadrilateral TUVW with matching sides and angles in the same order. Prove they are congruent.

example.problem: Two quadrilaterals have all matching sides and angles. Are they congruent?
example.solution: Yes. All four sides match and all four angles match. The quadrilaterals are congruent.

slides.inSimpleWords: For any polygon, equal sides and angles mean congruence.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Two figures are congruent if they have the same size and shape.
For triangles: SSS, SAS, ASA, and AAS are the congruence rules.
For polygons, all sides and angles must match.
Reflection, rotation, and translation preserve congruence.
Congruent shapes are geometric twins — identical copies.

slides.inSimpleWords: Congruence is the geometry word for 'identical twins' — same size, same shape, every time.

image.alt: What We Learned — Geometric Twins

subject: Mathematics
title: The Temperature Game
hook: Ravi tracks temperature changes in Delhi using positive and negative numbers, then learns to add, subtract, multiply, and divide them.

slides.title: The Temperature Game
slides.storyContext: In Delhi, winter temperatures drop below zero. Ravi and his grandfather use integers to track these changes.

slides.title: Below Zero
slides.storyContext: It's December in Delhi. Grandfather shows Ravi a thermometer. 'See, beta? Today it is 15°C. Yesterday was 8°C. But in January, it will drop to −2°C or even −5°C.' Ravi frowns. 'How can temperature be negative?' Grandfather smiles. 'It is just a number below zero. Let me teach you how integers work — they are positive, negative, and zero.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Integers are whole numbers that can be positive (above zero), negative (below zero), or zero itself.

slides.title: What are Integers?

points.text: Integers are whole numbers: ..., −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...
Positive integers are greater than zero: 1, 2, 3, ...
Negative integers are less than zero: −1, −2, −3, ...
Zero is neither positive nor negative.

example.problem: Write the temperature changes in Delhi as integers. Morning: 10°C. Evening: −3°C. Night: −8°C.
example.solution: Morning = 10. Evening = −3. Night = −8. All are integers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Integers are numbers on a number line: negatives on the left of zero, positives on the right.

slides.title: The Number Line Adventure
slides.storyContext: Grandfather draws a number line. 'Ravi, this line shows all integers. Zero is in the middle. Positives go right, negatives go left. Positive 5 is 5 steps to the right. Negative 5 is 5 steps to the left.' Ravi visualizes marching along the line.
slides.inSimpleWords: The number line is a visual way to understand positive and negative integers.

slides.title: Absolute Value

points.text: Absolute value is the distance from zero on the number line, always positive.
Denoted by |x|. Example: |−5| = 5, |5| = 5.
It tells you 'how far' a number is from zero, regardless of direction.

example.problem: Find |−7| and |7|.
example.solution: |−7| = 7 and |7| = 7. Both are 7 steps away from zero.

slides.inSimpleWords: Absolute value ignores the sign and tells you distance from zero.

slides.title: Adding Integers

points.text: When adding two positive integers: add them normally. 3 + 5 = 8.
When adding two negative integers: add their absolute values and put a negative sign. (−3) + (−5) = −8.
When adding a positive and a negative: find the difference and keep the sign of the larger absolute value. 3 + (−5) = −2.

example.problem: The temperature was 5°C. It dropped 12°C. What is the new temperature?
example.solution: 5 + (−12) = −7. The new temperature is −7°C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Adding a negative is like moving left on the number line; adding positive moves right.

slides.title: Adding Positives and Negatives
slides.storyContext: Ravi practices: Start at +3. Add −5. Where do we end up?

example.solution: Start at 3, move 5 steps left: 3 → 2 → 1 → 0 → −1 → −2. Answer: −2.

slides.inSimpleWords: When adding a negative, move left on the number line.

slides.title: Subtracting Integers

points.text: Subtraction of integers can be rewritten as addition of the opposite. a − b = a + (−b).
Remember: subtracting a negative is like adding a positive.

example.problem: The temperature was −5°C. It rose by 12°C. What is the new temperature?
example.solution: (−5) − (−12) = (−5) + 12 = 7. The new temperature is 7°C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Subtraction of integers is really addition of the opposite number.

slides.title: The Subtraction Trick
slides.storyContext: Grandfather tells Ravi: 'Subtraction is a trick! To subtract, just add the opposite. Subtracting −5 is the same as adding +5. Makes sense?' Ravi nods as he understands the pattern.
slides.inSimpleWords: Subtract by adding the opposite — it's a shortcut to make math easier.

slides.title: Adding Two Negatives

points.text: When both integers are negative, add their absolute values and keep the negative sign.
Think of it as losing money twice — you end up more in debt.

example.problem: The temperature dropped 3°C, then dropped another 4°C. What is the total change?
example.solution: (−3) + (−4) = −7. Total drop is 7°C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Adding two negatives gives a bigger negative.

slides.title: Multiplying Integers

points.text: Positive × Positive = Positive. 3 × 5 = 15.
Negative × Negative = Positive. (−3) × (−5) = 15.
Positive × Negative = Negative. 3 × (−5) = −15.
Negative × Positive = Negative. (−3) × 5 = −15.

example.problem: The temperature drops 3°C every hour for 5 hours. What is the total change?
example.solution: (−3) × 5 = −15. The temperature has dropped 15°C.

slides.inSimpleWords: When multiplying integers: same signs give positive; different signs give negative.

slides.title: Multiplication Practice
slides.storyContext: Ravi multiplies (−4) × (−3). Two negatives multiplying together.

example.solution: Negative × Negative = Positive. (−4) × (−3) = 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: Two negatives make a positive — remember this key rule.

slides.title: Dividing Integers

points.text: The rules for division are the same as multiplication.
Positive ÷ Positive = Positive. 15 ÷ 3 = 5.
Negative ÷ Negative = Positive. (−15) ÷ (−3) = 5.
Positive ÷ Negative = Negative. 15 ÷ (−3) = −5.
Negative ÷ Positive = Negative. (−15) ÷ 3 = −5.

example.problem: Over 5 hours, the temperature dropped 20°C. What is the average drop per hour?
example.solution: (−20) ÷ 5 = −4. The average drop is 4°C per hour.

slides.inSimpleWords: Division of integers follows the same positive/negative rules as multiplication.

slides.title: Division with Negatives
slides.storyContext: Ravi divides (−24) ÷ (−4). Two negatives dividing.

example.solution: Negative ÷ Negative = Positive. (−24) ÷ (−4) = 6.

slides.inSimpleWords: Division follows multiplication rules — two negatives give positive.

slides.title: Temperature Drops Over Days
slides.storyContext: Ravi tracks a temperature drop. If the total drop over 3 days is −15°C, what is the average drop per day? Grandfather guides: '−15 ÷ 3 = −5. Each day dropped 5°C.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Division finds the per-unit rate — useful for averaging changes.

slides.title: Order of Operations with Integers (PEMDAS)

points.text: Follow PEMDAS: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division (left to right), Addition/Subtraction (left to right).
Example: 5 + 3 × (−2) = 5 + (−6) = −1. (Multiply before adding.)
Example: (−8 + 3) × 2 = (−5) × 2 = −10. (Parentheses first.)

example.problem: Calculate: 10 − 2 × (−3) + 4.

slides.inSimpleWords: Follow the order: Parentheses → Exponents → Multiply/Divide → Add/Subtract.

slides.title: Multi-Step Integer Operations
slides.storyContext: Ravi practices a complex calculation: (−5) × 2 + 8 ÷ (−4). He carefully follows order of operations.
slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply and divide first (left to right), then add and subtract.

slides.title: A Week of Temperature Changes
slides.storyContext: Ravi records: Monday +2°, Tuesday −3°, Wednesday −1°, Thursday +4°, Friday −2°. He adds them step by step to find the week's net change.
slides.inSimpleWords: Real-world problems often need multiple operations in sequence.

slides.title: Grandfather's Weather Challenge
slides.storyContext: Grandfather gives Ravi a puzzle: 'Monday was 8°C. Tuesday dropped 12°C. Wednesday rose 5°C. Then we had 4 nights each losing 3°C. What was the temperature after those 4 nights?'

example.problem: Calculate: Start at 8. Subtract 12. Add 5. Subtract (3 × 4).

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine operations step by step: add the positives, add the negatives, then find the difference.

slides.title: Can You Solve This?
slides.storyContext: Ravi's weather diary: Monday was −3°C. Over 6 days, the temperature changed by: +2, −4, +1, −5, +3, −2 (in °C each day). What is the final temperature?

example.problem: Start: −3. Changes: +2, −4, +1, −5, +3, −2. Final temperature?

slides.inSimpleWords: Group positive and negative changes, then combine to find the final result.

slides.title: Advanced Challenge: Mixed Operations
slides.storyContext: Ravi faces a complex problem: Start at −5°C. Double the temperature (multiply by 2), then add 8. What is the result?

example.solution: First multiply: (−5) × 2 = −10. Then add: −10 + 8 = −2.

slides.inSimpleWords: When mixing operations, follow PEMDAS — multiplication and division before addition and subtraction.

slides.title: Complex Integer Puzzle
slides.storyContext: Ravi solves: −20 ÷ (−4) − 3 × 2 + (−6). Multiple operations at once.
slides.inSimpleWords: Handle division and multiplication left to right, then subtraction and addition.

slides.title: Real-World Banking Problem
slides.storyContext: Ravi thinks about money: 'If I start with −100 rupees (debt), earn 50 rupees, then earn another 80 rupees, what's my final balance?'

example.problem: Start: −100. Add 50. Add 80. Final balance?
example.solution: (−100) + 50 + 80 = (−100) + 130 = 30 rupees (positive balance now).

slides.inSimpleWords: Real-world problems like debt and earning use integer addition and subtraction.

slides.title: Properties of Integer Operations

points.text: Commutative Property: a + b = b + a and a × b = b × a (order doesn't matter for + and ×).
Associative Property: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) (grouping doesn't matter).
Distributive Property: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c.

example.solution: Left: (−3) × 7 = −21. Right: −15 + (−6) = −21. Both equal.

slides.inSimpleWords: Math properties help you simplify and reorganize integer calculations.

slides.title: Using Distributive Property

example.problem: Calculate 6 × (−2 + 3) using the distributive property.

slides.inSimpleWords: Distribute the outside number to each term inside the parentheses.

slides.title: Comparing and Ordering Integers

points.text: Integers on a number line increase from left to right.
−5 < −2 < 0 < 3 < 7 (less than relationships).
Use < (less than), > (greater than), = (equal) to compare.

example.problem: Order from smallest to largest: −5, 0, 3, −2, 7.

slides.inSimpleWords: On the number line, left is smaller; right is larger.

slides.title: Comparing Integer Temperatures
slides.storyContext: Ravi compares winter temperatures: −8°C vs −3°C. Which is colder?

example.problem: Which is colder: −8°C or −3°C?
example.solution: −8°C is colder because −8 < −3 (further left on the number line).

slides.inSimpleWords: More negative means colder — further left on the number line.

slides.title: Multi-Step Real-World Challenge
slides.storyContext: Ravi's bank account started at −50 rupees. He earned 200 rupees, spent 75 rupees, then earned 120 rupees. What is his final balance?
slides.inSimpleWords: Track income and expenses step by step to find the final balance.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Integers include positive, negative, and zero.
Adding integers: use sign rules (same signs, different signs).
Subtracting integers: convert to addition of the opposite.
Multiplying/dividing integers: same signs give positive; different signs give negative.
Combine operations step by step using order of operations (PEMDAS).

slides.inSimpleWords: Integer operations follow sign rules: positive-positive and negative-negative are positive; mixed signs are negative.

subject: Mathematics
title: Dividing the Harvest
hook: A farmer needs to divide 24 baskets of wheat and 36 baskets of rice equally among workers, and finds the largest group size possible.

slides.title: Dividing the Harvest
slides.storyContext: On a farm in Punjab, Farmer Gopal must distribute grain baskets fairly among workers.

slides.title: The Fair Share
slides.storyContext: Harvest season has arrived. Farmer Gopal has 24 baskets of wheat and 36 baskets of rice. He wants to divide them equally among workers without leaving any baskets unopened or wasting grain. Anita asks: 'Dad, what if we hire 6 workers? Can we divide evenly?' Gopal thinks hard. 'Not sure, beta. Let me find a number that divides both perfectly. That would be fair to everyone.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Finding numbers that divide evenly into two quantities is about finding common factors.

slides.title: Factors and Divisors

points.text: A factor of a number divides it exactly with no remainder.

example.problem: List all factors of 24.
example.solution: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Each divides 24 with remainder 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Factors are numbers that divide evenly into another number with no leftover.

image.alt: Factors and Divisors — Finding Common Ground

slides.title: Anita Tests Factors
slides.storyContext: Anita writes down: 'If Dad has 24 baskets of wheat, he could divide among 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, or 24 workers. All these are factors of 24. With 5 workers, there would be leftover baskets — 5 is not a factor of 24.'
slides.inSimpleWords: A factor divides perfectly; a non-factor leaves remainder.

slides.title: Testing Divisibility

points.text: A number is divisible by 2 if it is even (ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8).
A number is divisible by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3.
A number is divisible by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5.
These rules help quickly identify factors.

example.problem: Is 36 divisible by 3?
example.solution: Sum of digits: 3 + 6 = 9. Since 9 is divisible by 3, yes, 36 is divisible by 3.

slides.inSimpleWords: Divisibility rules let you quickly check if a number is a factor.

slides.title: Common Factors

points.text: A common factor is a number that divides two or more numbers evenly.
Common factors of 24 and 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.
These six numbers divide both 24 and 36 with no remainder.

example.problem: Find common factors of 24 and 36.

slides.inSimpleWords: Common factors divide multiple numbers at the same time.

image.alt: Common Factors — Finding Common Ground

slides.title: Testing Common Factors
slides.storyContext: Anita checks: 'If we hire 6 workers, can we divide both 24 wheat and 36 rice equally? Let's see: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 baskets per worker. 36 ÷ 6 = 6 baskets per worker. Yes! 6 is a common factor.'

example.problem: Is 6 a common factor of 24 and 36?
example.solution: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 (no remainder). 36 ÷ 6 = 6 (no remainder). Yes, 6 is a common factor.

slides.inSimpleWords: Check if a number divides both quantities evenly.

slides.title: Greatest Common Factor (GCF)

points.text: The Greatest Common Factor (GCF) is the largest number that divides two or more numbers evenly.
GCF of 24 and 36 is 12 (the largest common factor).
If we divide both by their GCF: 24 ÷ 12 = 2, and 36 ÷ 12 = 3.

example.problem: Find the GCF of 24 and 36.
example.solution: Common factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The greatest is 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: The GCF is the biggest number that divides both quantities evenly.

image.alt: Greatest Common Factor (GCF) — Finding Common Ground

slides.title: Finding the Maximum Workers
slides.storyContext: Anita declares: 'Dad, the GCF of 24 and 36 is 12. That means you can hire 12 workers, and each gets exactly 2 baskets of wheat and 3 baskets of rice. That's the fairest way!' Gopal smiles: 'Perfect, beta!'
slides.inSimpleWords: The GCF tells us the maximum number of equal groups we can make.

slides.title: Finding GCF Using Prime Factorization

points.text: Prime factorization breaks a number into prime factors (numbers only divisible by 1 and themselves).
GCF = 2² × 3 = 12 (take the lowest power of each common prime).

example.problem: Find GCF of 24 and 36 using prime factorization.
example.solution: 24 = 2³ × 3. 36 = 2² × 3². Common primes: 2² and 3¹. GCF = 2² × 3 = 4 × 3 = 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: Prime factorization shows which primes are shared; multiply the shared ones (in lowest power) to get the GCF.

slides.title: Prime Factorization Practice
slides.storyContext: Anita draws a factor tree for 36. She breaks it down: 36 = 6 × 6 = (2 × 3) × (2 × 3) = 2² × 3².

example.problem: Find the prime factorization of 36.

slides.inSimpleWords: Break a number into prime factors by repeatedly dividing by primes.

slides.title: Using GCF to Simplify Fractions

points.text: The GCF helps us simplify fractions and divide quantities fairly.
To reduce a fraction: divide both numerator and denominator by their GCF.

example.problem: Simplify 18/30.

slides.inSimpleWords: Dividing both top and bottom by their GCF makes a fraction simpler.

slides.title: Simplifying Gopal's Ratio
slides.storyContext: Anita simplifies the ratio of wheat to rice: 24 to 36. Using the GCF of 12: 24/36 = 2/3. So each worker gets 2 wheat to 3 rice — a 2:3 ratio.

example.problem: Simplify the ratio 24:36.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ratios can be simplified using the GCF.

slides.title: Gopal's Worker Distribution
slides.storyContext: Farmer Gopal decides to use the GCF. He has 24 baskets of wheat and 36 baskets of rice. He wants to hire the maximum number of workers such that each gets an equal share.

example.problem: If Gopal uses the GCF to divide, how many workers should he hire? How many baskets of wheat and rice does each get?
example.solution: GCF of 24 and 36 is 12. So hire 12 workers. Each gets 24 ÷ 12 = 2 baskets of wheat and 36 ÷ 12 = 3 baskets of rice.

slides.inSimpleWords: The GCF tells us the maximum number of equal groups we can make.

slides.title: Finding GCF Using the Euclidean Algorithm

points.text: The Euclidean algorithm repeatedly divides the larger number by the smaller.
Replace the larger with the smaller, and the smaller with the remainder.
When remainder is 0, the other number is the GCF.

example.problem: Find GCF(48, 18) using the Euclidean algorithm.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Euclidean algorithm is a fast way to find GCF by repeated division.

slides.title: Can You Solve This?
slides.storyContext: Anita's school has 48 red pens and 60 blue pens. The teacher wants to pack them into identical gift boxes, with no pens left over and no mixing of colors. What is the maximum number of boxes the teacher can make? How many red and blue pens go in each box?

example.problem: Find GCF of 48 and 60, then determine box count and contents.
example.solution: GCF of 48 and 60 is 12. So 12 boxes. Each box has 48 ÷ 12 = 4 red pens and 60 ÷ 12 = 5 blue pens.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the GCF to find the maximum number of equal groups (boxes).

slides.title: Advanced Challenge: Multiple Groups
slides.storyContext: Gopal now has 40 apples, 60 oranges, and 80 mangoes. He wants to pack them into identical boxes with no fruit left over. What is the GCF, and how many boxes can he make?

example.problem: Find GCF of 40, 60, and 80.
example.solution: 40 = 2³ × 5, 60 = 2² × 3 × 5, 80 = 2⁴ × 5. GCF = 2² × 5 = 20. He can make 20 boxes. Each has 2 apples, 3 oranges, 4 mangoes.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCF works for three or more numbers too — find the common prime factors with lowest powers.

slides.title: Real-World GCF Challenge
slides.storyContext: A community center has 72 sport balls and 90 cones. They want to create identical sports kits with no equipment left over. What is the maximum number of kits? How many balls and cones in each?

example.problem: Find GCF of 72 and 90, then determine kit count and contents.
example.solution: 72 = 2³ × 3². 90 = 2 × 3² × 5. GCF = 2 × 3² = 18. So 18 kits. Each has 72 ÷ 18 = 4 balls and 90 ÷ 18 = 5 cones.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCF solves real fair-sharing problems in sports, classrooms, and community settings.

slides.title: Least Common Multiple (LCM)

points.text: The Least Common Multiple (LCM) is the smallest number divisible by two or more numbers.
LCM of 6 and 8: Multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, ... Multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24, ... LCM = 24.
LCM is useful for finding common denominators in fractions.

example.problem: Find LCM of 6 and 8.
example.solution: Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24. Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. LCM = 24.

slides.inSimpleWords: The LCM is the smallest number that both numbers divide into evenly.

slides.title: LCM in Real Life
slides.storyContext: Gopal's buses arrive: one every 6 days, another every 8 days. When will they both arrive on the same day?

example.problem: Find LCM of 6 and 8 to determine when buses arrive together.
example.solution: LCM of 6 and 8 is 24. The buses will arrive together every 24 days.

slides.inSimpleWords: LCM helps solve scheduling and repeated-event problems.

slides.title: LCM Using Prime Factorization

points.text: To find LCM: list prime factors of each number and take the HIGHEST power of each prime.
Compare to GCF: GCF uses lowest powers; LCM uses highest powers.

example.problem: Find LCM of 12 and 18 using prime factorization.

slides.inSimpleWords: For LCM, multiply the highest power of each prime factor.

slides.title: GCF vs LCM Comparison
slides.storyContext: Anita notices: GCF and LCM are related opposites. GCF finds the biggest shared divisor; LCM finds the smallest shared multiple.

example.problem: For 24 and 36: find both GCF and LCM.
example.solution: GCF = 12 (biggest divisor of both). LCM = 72 (smallest multiple of both). Note: 12 × 72 = 24 × 36 = 864.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCF ÷ into; LCM × into — opposite operations.

slides.title: Coprime Numbers

points.text: Two numbers are coprime (or relatively prime) if their GCF is 1.
Example: 15 and 28 are coprime (GCF = 1).
Coprime numbers share no common factors except 1.

example.problem: Are 15 and 28 coprime?
example.solution: Factors of 15: 1, 3, 5, 15. Factors of 28: 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 28. Only common factor is 1. Yes, coprime.

slides.inSimpleWords: Coprime numbers have nothing in common except 1.

slides.title: Real-World Fraction Simplification
slides.storyContext: Anita needs to simplify 28/42. She finds GCF(28, 42) = 14, so 28/42 = 2/3.

example.problem: Simplify 28/42.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use GCF to reduce fractions to simplest form.

slides.title: GCF and LCM Combined Challenge
slides.storyContext: Gopal has two tasks: Pack 30 red ribbons and 45 blue ribbons into boxes (GCF problem). Schedule two workers who work every 20 days and 30 days (LCM problem).

example.problem: Find GCF(30, 45) for boxes. Find LCM(20, 30) for scheduling.
example.solution: GCF(30, 45) = 15 boxes. LCM(20, 30) = 60 days until both work together again.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use GCF for dividing groups; use LCM for synchronizing schedules.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: A factor divides a number evenly with no remainder.
A common factor divides two or more numbers evenly.
The GCF is the greatest common factor — the largest number dividing all given numbers.
Prime factorization and division methods both find the GCF.
The GCF simplifies fractions, finds equal distributions, and solves real-world fair-sharing problems.

slides.inSimpleWords: The GCF is the key to dividing quantities fairly and simplifying fractions.

image.alt: What We Learned — Finding Common Ground

subject: Mathematics
title: Rajesh's Treasure Map
hook: Rajesh uses a grid to locate a hidden treasure box at home, learning about the coordinate plane and how to find points.

characters.name: Rajesh
characters.role: class-7 student who loves treasure hunts

slides.title: Rajesh's Treasure Map
slides.storyContext: Grandmother hides a box in her house and gives Rajesh a grid to find it.

slides.title: The Treasure Hunt
slides.storyContext: Rajesh's grandmother loves games. She draws a grid on a piece of paper. 'Beta, this grid shows my house. The treasure is hidden at a specific spot. I will give you two clues: move 3 steps to the right and 2 steps up. That is where you must dig!' Rajesh looks confused. 'How do I translate that to the paper?' Grandmother smiles and teaches him coordinates.
slides.inSimpleWords: A coordinate grid uses two numbers to describe exactly where a point is: one for right-left, one for up-down.

image.alt: The Treasure Hunt — Another Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: What is a Coordinate?

points.text: A coordinate is a pair of numbers that pinpoints an exact location on a grid.
Think of it like an address: 'third floor, apartment 5B' tells you exactly where someone lives.
On a map, coordinates help rescue teams find lost hikers, or delivery people find your house.

slides.inSimpleWords: A coordinate is like a home address but for points on a grid—it tells you exactly where to find something.

slides.title: The Coordinate Plane

points.text: A coordinate plane is a grid with two perpendicular lines: the x-axis (horizontal) and y-axis (vertical).
They meet at the origin (0, 0).
The x-axis goes left and right; the y-axis goes up and down.

example.problem: Name the axes of a coordinate plane.
example.solution: The horizontal axis is the x-axis. The vertical axis is the y-axis. They meet at the origin (0, 0).

slides.inSimpleWords: The coordinate plane is like a chessboard with horizontal and vertical lines that help you find exact locations.

slides.title: Rajesh Learns to Count
slides.storyContext: Rajesh stands at the center of the grid. Grandmother points. 'Do you see the middle point, where the lines cross? That is zero-zero, or the origin. Now, count 3 squares to the right. Then count 2 squares up. That is where the treasure is!' Rajesh carefully counts and marks the spot.
slides.inSimpleWords: Start at the center (origin), count right or left for the first number, count up or down for the second number.

slides.title: Ordered Pairs

points.text: A point on the coordinate plane is described by an ordered pair (x, y).
x is the horizontal distance from the origin (positive to the right, negative to the left).
y is the vertical distance from the origin (positive up, negative down).
The order matters: (3, 2) is different from (2, 3).

example.problem: Write the ordered pair for a point 4 units to the right and 3 units up from the origin.
example.solution: (4, 3). The first number is x (horizontal); the second is y (vertical).

slides.inSimpleWords: An ordered pair (x, y) tells you exactly how far right and how far up a point is.

slides.title: A Tricky Second Clue
slides.storyContext: Rajesh finds the first treasure and returns to Grandmother. 'Well done! Now here is a harder one. Imagine I moved some treasures left and down instead of right and up. If I say "3 steps left and 2 steps down," what would you write?' Rajesh thinks hard. 'Left is the opposite of right... and down is the opposite of up. So it would be negative!' Grandmother claps. 'Exactly! You are ready for negative coordinates.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Negative numbers on a coordinate plane mean going left or down from the origin.

slides.title: Positive and Negative Coordinates

points.text: Positive x: move right from the origin.
Negative x: move left from the origin.
Positive y: move up from the origin.
Negative y: move down from the origin.
Examples: (3, 2) is right-up; (−2, 4) is left-up; (−3, −2) is left-down.

example.problem: Write coordinates for a point 2 units left and 5 units down.
example.solution: (−2, −5). Left = negative x, down = negative y.

slides.inSimpleWords: Positive x and y go right and up. Negative x and y go left and down.

slides.title: Quadrants

points.text: The coordinate plane is divided into four quadrants by the axes.
Quadrant I: x positive, y positive (top-right).
Quadrant II: x negative, y positive (top-left).
Quadrant III: x negative, y negative (bottom-left).
Quadrant IV: x positive, y negative (bottom-right).

example.problem: In which quadrant is the point (−2, 3)?
example.solution: x is negative (−2), y is positive (3). This is Quadrant II (top-left).

slides.inSimpleWords: Each quadrant has a name based on whether x and y are positive or negative.

slides.title: Quadrants in the House
slides.storyContext: Grandmother divides her house into four sections using the middle point as the origin. 'The treasures are scattered in all four sections, beta. Some are in the front-right, some in the back-left, some below the floorboards. Each section is a quadrant. Your task is to find one treasure in each quadrant!' Rajesh grabs his pencil and begins mapping.
slides.inSimpleWords: A house divided by a center point creates four zones—just like the four quadrants on a coordinate plane.

slides.title: Naming Quadrants by Sign
slides.storyContext: Rajesh learns a trick to remember quadrants. Quadrant I is (+, +), Quadrant II is (−, +), Quadrant III is (−, −), and Quadrant IV is (+, −).

example.problem: List all four quadrants and their signs for x and y.

slides.inSimpleWords: Remember quadrants by their signs: top-right is both positive, top-left is x negative-y positive, and so on.

slides.title: Plotting Points

points.text: To plot a point (x, y), start at the origin.
Move right (positive x) or left (negative x) by x units.
Then move up (positive y) or down (negative y) by y units.
Mark the spot where you land.

example.problem: Plot the point (3, 2) on a coordinate plane.
example.solution: Start at origin (0, 0). Move 3 units right. Then move 2 units up. Plot the point.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plotting is like following directions: first go right/left, then go up/down.

slides.title: Rajesh Practices Plotting
slides.storyContext: Grandmother gives Rajesh five clues. 'Plot these treasures: (1, 2), (−2, 3), (3, −1), (−1, −2), and (0, 0). Mark each one. The one at the origin is the golden coin! The others are gemstones.' Rajesh works methodically, starting at the origin, counting carefully in each direction.
slides.inSimpleWords: Practice plotting by counting: start at (0, 0), move horizontally first, then vertically.

slides.title: Reading a Point from the Graph

points.text: If a point is already plotted, find its coordinates by dropping vertical and horizontal lines to the axes.
The x-coordinate is where the vertical line hits the x-axis.
The y-coordinate is where the horizontal line hits the y-axis.

example.problem: A point is 4 units right of the origin and 2 units up. Write its coordinates.
example.solution: The coordinates are (4, 2).

slides.inSimpleWords: To read a point's coordinates, look where it lines up with the x-axis and y-axis.

image.alt: Reading a Point from the Graph — Another Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: Finding Treasures by Reading Coordinates
slides.storyContext: Now Grandmother shows Rajesh a map with treasures already marked as dots. 'These dots are treasures I hid last year. Can you tell me where each one is by reading the coordinates from the map?' Rajesh learns to reverse the process: instead of plotting from coordinates, he reads coordinates from a plot.
slides.inSimpleWords: When you see a plotted point, you can read its coordinates by checking its position relative to both axes.

slides.title: Grandmother's Treasure Locations
slides.storyContext: Grandmother gives Rajesh several clues. The treasure room has treasures at: (2, 3), (−1, 2), (3, −2), and (−2, −3). Plot them and name their quadrants.

example.problem: Plot (2, 3), (−1, 2), (3, −2), (−2, −3). State their quadrants.
example.solution: (2, 3): Quadrant I. (−1, 2): Quadrant II. (3, −2): Quadrant IV. (−2, −3): Quadrant III.

slides.inSimpleWords: By plotting multiple points, you can see patterns and find hidden treasures on a map.

image.alt: Grandmother's Treasure Locations — Another Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: The Grand Challenge
slides.storyContext: Grandmother smiles. 'One final test, beta. I have hidden the greatest treasure—the Family Heirloom Necklace—at a secret location on this map. You must use everything you have learned to find it.' She gives him a grid and a single coordinate: (−4, 4). Rajesh feels the weight of the challenge.
slides.inSimpleWords: A coordinate plane is not just a game—it is a real tool to navigate and find things in the world.

slides.title: Real-World Uses of Coordinates

points.label: Treasure hunts and maps
points.text: Ancient and modern maps use coordinate grids (latitude and longitude) to locate places.

points.label: Video games
points.text: Characters move on coordinate planes—a player's position is stored as (x, y).

points.label: GPS systems
points.text: Every location on Earth is identified by coordinates (latitude, longitude).

points.label: Architecture and construction
points.text: Buildings are designed on coordinate grids to ensure precise placement of rooms and structures.

slides.inSimpleWords: Coordinates are used to pinpoint locations in real life—from maps to games to GPS.

slides.title: Can You Solve This?
slides.storyContext: Rajesh's grandmother says: 'Four treasures are hidden. First, move 5 steps right and 4 steps up. That is clue 1. Clue 2: 3 steps left and 2 steps up. Clue 3: 2 steps right and 5 steps down. Clue 4: 4 steps left and 3 steps down.' Write the ordered pairs for all four treasures.

example.problem: Convert Grandmother's directions to ordered pairs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert word clues to coordinates: right/left is x, up/down is y.

image.alt: Can You Solve This? — Another Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: Rajesh Finds the Heirloom
slides.storyContext: Rajesh carefully places his pencil at the origin. He counts 4 steps left (negative x) and 4 steps up (positive y). He marks the spot: (−4, 4). The coordinate points to a loose tile on Grandmother's floor. He lifts it and finds the necklace! His eyes shine. Grandmother embraces him. 'You have mastered the coordinate plane, beta. Now you can find anything on a map—or navigate anywhere in the world.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Once you understand coordinates, you can find anything and navigate anywhere using just two numbers.

slides.title: Distance Between Two Points

points.text: Once you have coordinates for two points, you can find the distance between them.
If the points are (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂), the distance is √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²].
This is called the distance formula.

example.problem: Find the distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6).

slides.inSimpleWords: The distance formula uses coordinates to calculate how far apart two points are on a plane.

slides.title: Measuring Between Treasures
slides.storyContext: Rajesh discovers that two treasures are at (2, 3) and (5, 7). 'Grandmother, how far apart are these treasures?' Grandmother smiles and teaches him the distance formula. Rajesh realizes that coordinates do not just tell him where things are—they also tell him how far apart they are.
slides.inSimpleWords: Coordinates help you not only find things but also measure distances between them.

slides.title: Midpoint Between Two Points

points.text: The midpoint is the point exactly halfway between two other points.
If the two points are (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂), the midpoint is [(x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2].
You simply average the x-coordinates and the y-coordinates.

example.problem: Find the midpoint between (2, 4) and (8, 10).

slides.inSimpleWords: The midpoint is found by averaging the x and y coordinates of two points.

slides.title: The Meeting Point
slides.storyContext: Rajesh and his friend Priya each hide a treasure: Rajesh at (1, 1) and Priya at (9, 9). They want to meet exactly halfway. Using the midpoint formula, they find the meeting point at (5, 5). They plan to meet there tomorrow!
slides.inSimpleWords: If two people are at different coordinates, the midpoint helps them find where to meet.

slides.title: A Practical Grid Search
slides.storyContext: Rajesh imagines a larger treasure hunt across his village. Treasures are at (0, 0), (6, 0), (6, 6), and (0, 6)—the four corners of a square field. What is the center of this field?

example.problem: Find the center (midpoint) of a square with corners at (0, 0) and (6, 6).
example.solution: The center is the midpoint of the diagonal from (0, 0) to (6, 6): [(0+6)/2, (0+6)/2] = (3, 3).

slides.inSimpleWords: The midpoint formula works for any two points, helping you find meeting places or centers of regions.

slides.title: Symmetry on the Coordinate Plane

points.text: Two points are symmetric about the x-axis if they have the same x-coordinate but opposite y-coordinates.
Two points are symmetric about the y-axis if they have the same y-coordinate but opposite x-coordinates.
Example: (3, 4) and (3, −4) are symmetric about the x-axis.

slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetry on a coordinate plane means points that are mirror images across an axis.

slides.title: Symmetry in Grandmother's Garden
slides.storyContext: Rajesh plots the positions of trees in Grandmother's garden on a coordinate plane. He notices that some trees are placed symmetrically—if one tree is at (2, 3), another is at (2, −3) on the opposite side of the x-axis! This symmetry makes the garden beautiful and balanced.
slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetric arrangements are pleasing to the eye and often appear in nature and design.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: The coordinate plane has an x-axis (horizontal) and y-axis (vertical) that meet at the origin (0, 0).
An ordered pair (x, y) specifies a point's location.
The four quadrants are determined by positive/negative x and y.
To plot a point: start at origin, move x units horizontally, then y units vertically.
To read a point's coordinates: drop lines to both axes.
Distance formula and midpoint formula extend coordinate skills to measure and find meeting points.

slides.inSimpleWords: The coordinate plane is like a map grid—ordered pairs tell you exactly where to find things, and formulas help you measure and navigate.

image.alt: What We Learned — Another Peek Beyond the Point

subject: Mathematics
title: The City Graph
hook: Meera plots bus routes on a grid, creating a linear graph that shows relationships between distance and time.

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: class-7 student curious about real-world math

slides.title: The City Graph
slides.storyContext: Meera watches buses move through Mumbai and learns how to graph motion and relationships.

slides.title: The Bus Route
slides.storyContext: Uncle runs a bus company in Mumbai. He shows Meera a chart: 'Look, beta. At time 0, the bus is at kilometer 0. After 1 hour, it is at kilometer 50. After 2 hours, it is at kilometer 100.' Meera sees a pattern. 'The distance increases by 50 every hour!' Uncle smiles. 'Exactly! That is a linear relationship. Let me show you how to graph it.'
slides.inSimpleWords: When two quantities change together in a steady pattern, their relationship is linear and forms a straight line on a graph.

slides.title: Variables and Relationships

points.text: Two quantities that change together have a relationship.
The independent variable is what we control or what happens first (usually time, x).
The dependent variable depends on the independent variable (usually distance, y).
In the bus example: time is independent (x), distance is dependent (y).

example.problem: A bus travels 50 km per hour. Distance depends on time. Which is the independent variable?
example.solution: Time is independent (x). Distance is dependent (y) because it depends on how long we travel.

slides.inSimpleWords: One variable causes a change in the other—that second one is dependent.

slides.title: Meera Watches a Bus
slides.storyContext: Meera sits on the platform and watches a bus leave the station. Every hour, the bus travels exactly 50 km. 'So if I plot time on the bottom and distance on the side, I get a straight line!' Meera sketches on paper, plotting points for 0 hours, 1 hour, 2 hours, and 3 hours.
slides.inSimpleWords: When you plot pairs of connected values (time and distance, or x and y), you create a graph that shows the relationship.

slides.title: Tables and Patterns

points.text: Before graphing, you can organize x and y values in a table.
Look for patterns: does y increase by the same amount each time x increases?
If yes, the relationship is linear.

example.problem: Make a table for the bus: time (hours) and distance (km) for times 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
example.solution: Time: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Distance: 0, 50, 100, 150, 200. The distance increases by 50 for each hour—linear!

slides.inSimpleWords: A table helps you spot patterns before you draw a graph.

slides.title: Linear Equations

points.text: A linear equation describes a relationship that forms a straight line.
The simplest form is y = mx + b, where m is the slope and b is the y-intercept.
For the bus: distance = 50 × time, or y = 50x (b = 0 because the bus starts at 0 km).

example.problem: The bus travels at 50 km/hour starting from 0 km. Write the equation.
example.solution: y = 50x, where y is distance (km) and x is time (hours).

slides.inSimpleWords: A linear equation uses y and x to show how one quantity depends on another.

image.alt: Linear Equations — Connecting the Dots...

slides.title: Uncle Explains the Formula
slides.storyContext: Uncle draws on a whiteboard: 'y = 50x. What does this mean? y is the distance we want to find. 50 is how fast the bus travels—every hour, it goes 50 km. x is the time in hours. And there is no plus b because the bus starts at zero distance.' Meera nods. 'So if x = 3, then y = 50 times 3, which is 150 km!'
slides.inSimpleWords: The equation y = mx + b is a recipe: m is the speed, b is the starting point, and x is the input.

slides.title: Slope

points.text: Slope measures how steep a line is—how much y changes for every unit change in x.
Slope = (change in y) / (change in x) = rise / run.
In the bus route: for every 1 hour (x), distance (y) increases by 50 km. Slope = 50.
A positive slope means y increases as x increases. A negative slope means y decreases as x increases.

example.problem: If a bus is at 50 km after 1 hour and 100 km after 2 hours, what is the slope?

slides.inSimpleWords: Slope tells you how fast the dependent variable changes as the independent variable changes.

slides.title: Comparing Two Bus Routes
slides.storyContext: Meera realizes that not all buses travel at the same speed. Uncle shows her two routes: Route A goes 50 km/hour, and Route B goes 40 km/hour. 'Both are straight lines, but Route A is steeper because it travels faster.' Meera sketches both lines. She sees that a steeper line means a bigger slope, which means faster change.
slides.inSimpleWords: A steeper line means a larger slope—faster change. A gentle line means a smaller slope—slower change.

slides.title: Y-Intercept

points.text: The y-intercept is the value of y when x is 0 (where the line crosses the y-axis).
In y = 50x, the y-intercept is 0 (the bus starts at 0 km).
In y = 2x + 5, the y-intercept is 5.
The y-intercept tells you the starting point or initial value.

example.problem: A bus route: y = 40x + 10. What is the y-intercept, and what does it mean?
example.solution: The y-intercept is 10. It means the bus started 10 km away from the origin point.

slides.inSimpleWords: The y-intercept is the starting value when x equals zero.

slides.title: A Bus with a Head Start
slides.storyContext: Uncle points to a new bus route. 'This bus started 20 km away from the main station and then travels at 60 km/hour. The equation is y = 60x + 20. See? The +20 is where the bus started!' Meera understands. 'So even at time 0, the bus is not at 0 km; it is at 20 km!'
slides.inSimpleWords: If a bus or any line does not start at zero, the y-intercept tells you where it starts.

slides.title: Plotting a Linear Graph

points.text: To plot a line, find at least two points and draw a straight line through them.
Use the y-intercept (0, b) as your first point.
Use the slope to find a second point: move right 1 unit (or any distance), then up by the slope.
Example: y = 2x + 1. Start at (0, 1). Move 1 right, 2 up to (1, 3). Draw the line.

example.problem: Plot the line y = 3x. Find two points and draw the line.
example.solution: Point 1: (0, 0). Point 2: (1, 3). Draw a straight line through both.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plot two points using the equation, then connect them with a straight line.

slides.title: Meera Plots the Bus Route
slides.storyContext: Meera carefully draws a coordinate plane on graph paper. For the route y = 50x, she marks (0, 0). Then she counts right 1 hour and up 50 km to mark (1, 50). She draws a straight line through both points. 'Look, Uncle! The line shows the entire trip!' Uncle nods proudly.
slides.inSimpleWords: Once you plot two points, you can draw the entire line—and it shows the complete pattern for all time values.

slides.title: Reading Values from a Graph

points.text: Once a line is plotted, you can read any y-value by finding a point on the line at a given x-value.
Find x on the horizontal axis, go up to the line, then read the y-value on the vertical axis.
This is called 'using the graph to predict or find values'.

example.problem: For the route y = 50x, what distance has the bus traveled after 2.5 hours? Use the graph.
example.solution: Find x = 2.5 on the horizontal axis, go up to the line, read y = 125 km.

slides.inSimpleWords: A graph lets you find the answer to 'if x is this, what is y?' without doing the math again.

slides.title: Uncle's Bus Schedule
slides.storyContext: Uncle's bus leaves Mumbai at 6 AM. After t hours, the bus is at distance d = 60t + 20 (in km, the +20 is because it started 20 km out of the city). Plot this relationship for 0 to 5 hours.

example.problem: Graph d = 60t + 20 for t = 0 to 5.
example.solution: t=0: d=20. t=1: d=80. t=2: d=140. t=3: d=200. t=4: d=260. t=5: d=320. Plot these points and draw a straight line.

slides.inSimpleWords: Build a table of x and y values from the equation, plot them, and connect with a line.

slides.title: Finding When the Bus Arrives
slides.storyContext: Meera's friend lives 200 km away. She asks Uncle, 'When will the bus reach my house?' Using the equation y = 60x + 20, Uncle rearranges: 200 = 60x + 20. So 180 = 60x, and x = 3. 'The bus will arrive in 3 hours!' Using algebra and graphs together makes the answer clear.
slides.inSimpleWords: Linear equations help you answer real questions: how long until arrival, how far after time x, or what time for distance y.

slides.title: Non-Linear vs. Linear Relationships

points.label: Linear
points.text: A straight line on the graph. Both variables change at a constant rate.

points.label: Non-linear
points.text: A curved line on the graph. The rate of change is not constant—it speeds up or slows down.

points.label: Example of non-linear
points.text: A ball thrown in the air follows a curved path (parabola) because gravity accelerates it downward.

slides.inSimpleWords: If the graph is a straight line, the relationship is linear. If it curves, the relationship is non-linear.

slides.title: A Train That Accelerates
slides.storyContext: Meera learns that a different vehicle—a train—accelerates, meaning it goes faster and faster. Its distance equation is y = x². When Meera plots this, it forms a curve, not a line! 'This is not linear!' she exclaims. Uncle smiles. 'Right, beta. Not everything in the world is linear. But buses traveling at constant speed? That is linear.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Linear relationships are steady and constant. Real-world motion often curves because of acceleration or deceleration.

slides.title: Can You Solve This?
slides.storyContext: Meera receives two bus routes: Bus A follows y = 40x (starting at 0 km). Bus B follows y = 30x + 50 (starting 50 km away). After 2 hours, which bus is farther? Graph both lines on the same coordinate plane.

example.problem: At t=2, where is each bus? Plot both routes for t=0 to 4.
example.solution: Bus A at t=2: y=40(2)=80 km. Bus B at t=2: y=30(2)+50=110 km. Bus B is farther. Plot both lines: A goes through (0,0) and (2,80). B goes through (0,50) and (2,110).

slides.inSimpleWords: Compare two linear relationships by plotting both lines and reading their values.

slides.title: Meera Teaches Her Parents
slides.storyContext: At dinner, Meera explains everything to her parents. She draws graphs showing bus routes, slopes, and y-intercepts. 'See? These straight lines tell us when buses arrive, how far they travel, and how fast they go!' Her parents are amazed. 'Our daughter is a mathematician!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Linear graphs and equations are powerful tools for understanding and predicting real-world motion.

slides.title: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines

points.label: Parallel lines
points.text: Two lines with the same slope never cross. y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x + 5 are parallel (both slope = 2).

points.label: Perpendicular lines
points.text: Two lines whose slopes multiply to give −1 cross at a right angle. y = 2x and y = −½x are perpendicular.

example.problem: Are y = 3x + 2 and y = 3x − 5 parallel or perpendicular?
example.solution: Both have slope 3, so they are parallel. They never meet.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines have the same slope. Perpendicular lines' slopes multiply to −1.

slides.title: Two Parallel Bus Routes
slides.storyContext: Meera notices that two buses on the same schedule travel at the same speed but start from different stations. Their routes are parallel! 'If Bus A is always faster than Bus B at every point in time, but they travel at the same speed, they will never meet. That is what parallel means!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Two buses with the same speed are parallel routes—they stay the same distance apart forever.

slides.title: Slope-Intercept Form Practice
slides.storyContext: Meera practices identifying slopes and y-intercepts from equations. For y = 3x + 7, she quickly says: 'Slope = 3, y-intercept = 7.' For y = −2x + 4, she says: 'Slope = −2, y-intercept = 4. This line goes down!'

example.problem: For y = −5x + 15, identify the slope and y-intercept.
example.solution: Slope = −5, y-intercept = 15. The line has a negative slope (goes downward) and crosses the y-axis at (0, 15).

slides.inSimpleWords: In y = mx + b, m is always the slope and b is always the y-intercept.

slides.title: Writing Linear Equations from Two Points

points.text: If you know two points on a line, you can write its equation.
Step 1: Calculate slope m = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁).
Step 2: Use one point and m to find b: y = mx + b.
Step 3: Write the equation y = mx + b.

example.problem: Write the equation of a line through points (1, 3) and (3, 7).
example.solution: Slope m = (7 − 3)/(3 − 1) = 4/2 = 2. Using point (1, 3): 3 = 2(1) + b, so b = 1. Equation: y = 2x + 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: With two points, you can always find the slope and y-intercept, then write the equation.

slides.title: Real-World Graphing
slides.storyContext: Meera realizes that linear graphs are everywhere. The phone bill depends linearly on minutes used. Electricity costs depend on kilowatt-hours. Temperature trends follow linear patterns over time. Every real-world relationship that changes at a constant rate can be graphed as a line.
slides.inSimpleWords: Linear relationships appear throughout the real world—any steady change can be graphed as a straight line.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: A linear equation (y = mx + b) describes a relationship that forms a straight line.
Slope (m) is the rate of change—how much y changes per unit of x.
The y-intercept (b) is the starting value when x is 0.
To plot a line, find at least two points and connect them.
Linear graphs model real-world relationships like bus routes, temperature changes, and business profits.
Parallel lines never meet; perpendicular lines cross at right angles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Linear graphs show steady relationships—straight lines with a slope and a starting point. They help us understand and predict real-world motion.

image.alt: What We Learned — Connecting the Dots...

subject: Mathematics
title: Anvi's Tile Design Challenge
hook: Help a young architect design perfect tiles for her village festival stage using straightedges and compasses.

characters.name: Anvi
characters.role: geometry-loving student who dreams of designing buildings

characters.name: Rohan
characters.role: Anvi's friend who helps with the design project

slides.title: Constructions and Tilings: Anvi's Tile Design Challenge
The Festival Stage
slides.storyContext: Anvi's village is hosting Diwali celebrations, and the temple committee wants a beautiful tiled stage. Anvi volunteers to design the tile pattern, but there's a catch: she has only a straightedge (unmarked ruler) and a compass—no measuring tape. Guru Ramesh, the carpenter, says, "Geometry solves this. You don't need numbers; you need clever construction." Rohan watches eagerly as they begin.

slides.title: What Is a Geometric Construction?
slides.storyContext: Guru Ramesh opens his toolbox. "A construction," he explains, "is drawing shapes exactly—no guessing, no measuring with numbers. Only two tools: the straightedge to draw straight lines, and the compass to copy distances and draw circles."

points.label: Definition
points.text: A geometric construction uses only a straightedge and compass to create shapes with exact relationships (like equal sides or equal angles).

points.label: Why it matters
points.text: Architects and builders use constructions to scale designs from small to large without errors. In Anvi's case, she can construct the tile shape once, then repeat it perfectly.

slides.inSimpleWords: A construction is drawing a perfect shape using only a straight edge and compass—no numbers, no guessing.

slides.title: Anvi Learns the Compass
slides.storyContext: Guru Ramesh hands Anvi a compass. 'Watch. The needle point stays fixed, and the pencil arm draws a circle at a fixed distance. This radius can be copied—if I mark the distance between two points with the compass, I can draw an arc of the same distance anywhere else.' Rohan experiments and successfully draws two identical arcs. 'This is like copying with a photocopy machine!'
slides.inSimpleWords: A compass copies distances perfectly—you can use the same distance again and again without measuring.

slides.title: The Straightedge and Compass: Tools of Precision

points.text: A straightedge has no markings—it only draws straight lines, not measurements.
A compass has two legs: one sharp point (for the center) and one with pencil (for drawing).
Together, they can create any regular polygon if you know the techniques.

slides.inSimpleWords: These two simple tools are all you need to draw perfect shapes—no numbers, no measuring.

slides.title: Constructing an Equilateral Triangle
slides.storyContext: "Our tiles will be equilateral triangles," says Guru Ramesh. "That means all three sides are equal, and all angles are 60°. Watch how the compass does the work."

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Draw a line segment AB with the straightedge.

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Place the compass point at A, open it to length AB, and draw an arc above the line.

points.label: Step 3
points.text: Without changing the compass width, place the point at B and draw another arc that crosses the first arc at point C.

points.label: Step 4
points.text: Join A to C and B to C with the straightedge. Triangle ABC is equilateral.

example.problem: If AB = 5 cm, what can you say about AC and BC?
example.solution: AC = BC = AB = 5 cm because the compass kept the same width for all three arcs. All three sides equal means an equilateral triangle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use a compass to copy the distance, then draw two arcs that meet. Connect the points and you have a perfect triangle with all sides equal.

image.alt: Constructing an Equilateral Triangle — Constructions and Tilings

slides.title: Anvi Constructs Her First Triangle
slides.storyContext: Anvi draws a line segment for the base. She sets the compass to the length of this base and draws arcs from both ends. Where they meet, she marks point C. Connecting all three points, she has a perfect equilateral triangle! 'Guru Ramesh, I made it!' He smiles. 'And it has no numbers, just geometry.'
slides.inSimpleWords: An equilateral triangle has all sides equal and all angles 60 degrees—it is the most symmetric triangle.

slides.title: Constructing Another Triangle
slides.storyContext: Anvi practices by constructing a second equilateral triangle of a different size. She draws a longer base and repeats the compass technique. Soon she has two perfect triangles—one large, one small—and both are equilateral!

example.problem: Construct an equilateral triangle with a base of 3 cm using only compass and straightedge.
