example.solution: Draw base AB = 3 cm. Open compass to 3 cm, place at A, draw arc. Place at B (same radius), draw arc that intersects first arc at C. Join A-C and B-C. Triangle ABC is equilateral with all sides = 3 cm and all angles = 60°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Once you learn the technique, you can construct perfect equilateral triangles of any size.

slides.title: Constructing a Square
slides.storyContext: Rohan asks, "What if we want square tiles instead?" Guru Ramesh nods. "Good question. A square is trickier because we need right angles. Let me show you."

points.label: Method
points.text: Draw a line segment AB. At point A, construct a perpendicular using the compass and straightedge (using the property that a perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the circle's center). Mark point D on this perpendicular such that AD = AB. Similarly, mark C so that BC = AB and angle D = angle C = 90°. Join D to C.

points.label: Why it works
points.text: The compass ensures all sides are equal; the perpendicular ensures all angles are 90°.

slides.inSimpleWords: To build a square, first draw a line, then use compass arcs to create a perpendicular line of equal length, then complete the square.

image.alt: Constructing a Square — Constructions and Tilings

slides.title: Creating a Perpendicular
slides.storyContext: Guru Ramesh demonstrates. 'To make a right angle without a protractor, I need perpendicularity. I draw a line, then use the compass to find a point equidistant from two points on the line. That gives me a perpendicular.' Anvi watches closely as he executes each step. The perpendicular line is perfect, without any guessing.
slides.inSimpleWords: A perpendicular line is at a right angle (90 degrees). You can construct it using only a compass and straightedge.

slides.title: Bisecting an Angle
slides.storyContext: "Sometimes," Guru Ramesh continues, "we need to split an angle exactly in half. The compass can do that too."

points.label: Goal
points.text: To bisect (split) angle AOB into two equal angles.

points.label: Steps
points.text: 1. Place compass at O, draw an arc that crosses both rays OA and OB. Mark these points P and Q. 2. Place compass at P and Q (with the same radius), draw two arcs that intersect at a point M. 3. Draw ray OM. This ray bisects angle AOB.

points.label: Why it works
points.text: The compass arcs create equal distances, so triangle OPM is congruent to triangle OQM, making angle POM = angle QOM.

slides.inSimpleWords: To split an angle in half, use the compass to draw equal arcs from both sides of the angle, then find where they cross.

image.alt: Bisecting an Angle — Constructions and Tilings

slides.title: Bisecting for Beauty
slides.storyContext: Anvi thinks about her design. 'If I bisect angles, I can divide shapes into smaller, equal parts! That would create symmetric patterns!' Guru Ramesh nods. 'Yes, beta. Many beautiful patterns come from bisecting angles and constructing symmetric shapes.'
slides.inSimpleWords: By bisecting angles and copying distances, you can create complex, symmetric, beautiful patterns.

slides.title: What Are Tilings (Tessellations)?
slides.storyContext: Anvi sketches triangles on paper. "Look, Guru—if I repeat these triangles, they fit together with no gaps or overlaps!" Guru Ramesh smiles. "That's tiling, or tessellation. Nature does this all the time."

points.label: Definition
points.text: A tiling is a pattern where shapes fit together to cover a flat surface completely, with no gaps or overlaps.

points.label: Key fact
points.text: The interior angles of shapes that meet at each point must sum to exactly 360°.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Equilateral triangles (60° each; six fit at a point: 6 × 60° = 360°), squares (90° each; four fit: 4 × 90° = 360°), regular hexagons (120° each; three fit: 3 × 120° = 360°).

example.problem: Can you tile a floor with regular pentagons (each interior angle = 108°)?
example.solution: No. If you try to place pentagons at a point: 108° + 108° + 108° = 324°. The fourth corner leaves a gap of 36°. Pentagons don't tile the plane.

slides.inSimpleWords: A tiling is when shapes fit together like a puzzle with no gaps. The angles at every corner point must add up to 360°.

slides.title: Testing the Angle Rule
slides.storyContext: Rohan cuts out several cardboard equilateral triangles from Anvi's construction. Each angle is 60°. He arranges six triangles around a central point. 'They fit perfectly with no gaps!' Anvi calculates: '6 times 60 equals 360! The angles add up exactly!' She realizes this is why triangles tile so beautifully.
slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes tile perfectly when their angles around a point add up to exactly 360 degrees.

slides.title: Interior Angles of Regular Polygons

points.text: An equilateral triangle has three 60° angles.
A square has four 90° angles.
A regular pentagon has five 108° angles.
A regular hexagon has six 120° angles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each regular polygon has equal interior angles, and the sum depends on the number of sides.

slides.title: Regular Tilings
slides.storyContext: "There are only three perfect tilings," Guru Ramesh explains. "And nature chose all three for a reason."

points.label: Triangular tiling
points.text: Equilateral triangles (6 per point). Bees use this in honeycombs—maximizes space for honey!

points.label: Square tiling
points.text: Squares (4 per point). This tiles the simplest way—floors, tiles, checkerboards.

points.label: Hexagonal tiling
points.text: Regular hexagons (3 per point). Honeycombs again! Hexagons are nature's answer for strength and efficiency.

slides.inSimpleWords: Only three regular shapes tile perfectly: triangles, squares, and hexagons. Bees know this and use hexagons in their hives!

slides.title: Anvi Chooses Triangles for Her Stage
slides.storyContext: Anvi decides on triangular tiles. 'Triangles fit together perfectly, and six meet at every corner. It will be strong and beautiful!' She constructs one perfect equilateral triangle and makes a stencil. Now she can repeat it as many times as needed for the stage.
slides.inSimpleWords: Once you construct one perfect tile shape, you can copy it many times to cover any area.

slides.title: Anvi's Tile Design
slides.storyContext: Anvi decides on a hexagonal tiling for the stage—it's beautiful and strong. "If the hexagon has a side of 1 meter," she calculates, "then I can construct each tile with the compass, and repeat it across the entire stage."

example.problem: Anvi constructs a regular hexagon with side length 1 meter using only a compass and straightedge. If the stage is 6 meters × 6 meters, how many complete hexagons can she fit along one edge (assuming no gaps)?
example.solution: A regular hexagon with side 1 meter has a 'width' (distance across flats) of approximately √3 ≈ 1.73 meters. So along a 6-meter edge, she can fit about 6 ÷ 1.73 ≈ 3 to 4 hexagons, depending on orientation. The exact number depends on how she arranges them—hexagonal tiling lets her nestle them efficiently.

slides.title: The Grand Pattern
slides.storyContext: Anvi and Rohan carefully place triangular tiles on the stage. Each triangle is identical, constructed using Anvi's compass and straightedge technique. The pattern is flawless—no gaps, no overlaps. Village members gather, amazed at the precision and beauty. 'This is mathematics in action!' says Guru Ramesh.
slides.inSimpleWords: Perfect constructions and correct tiling rules create beautiful, precise patterns that last for generations.

slides.title: Semi-Regular Tilings (Archimedean Tilings)

points.text: Beyond the three regular tilings, there are tilings using combinations of regular shapes.
Example: a tiling of triangles and squares together (in a specific pattern) can tile the plane.
The key is still that angles around every point must sum to exactly 360°.

example.problem: Can a pattern of triangles (60°) and squares (90°) tile the plane?
example.solution: Yes, if arranged correctly: 2 triangles (120°) + 1 square (90°) + another square (90°) + half another shape... Actually, yes: 2 triangles + 2 squares = 120° + 180° = 300°, so we need 60° more = 1 triangle. One valid arrangement uses 4 triangles and 2 squares at some points.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can mix shapes in tilings as long as the angles around each point add up to 360 degrees.

slides.title: Anvi's Next Challenge
slides.storyContext: The village elder approaches Anvi. 'Your triangle pattern is beautiful! But the next temple has a larger stage. Can you design a pattern using two different shapes?' Anvi thinks hard. 'I can combine squares and triangles if the angles add up to 360°!' Guru Ramesh smiles. 'That is the mark of a true mathematician, beta.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Once you master single-shape tilings, you can combine shapes to create even more complex and beautiful patterns.

slides.title: Why Only Three Regular Tilings?

points.text: A tiling works only if interior angles at each point sum to 360°.
Equilateral triangles: 6 × 60° = 360°. ✓
Pentagons: 108° × 3 = 324°; 108° × 4 = 432°. Neither works!

slides.inSimpleWords: Only three regular polygons can tile because their angles happen to divide 360° evenly.

slides.title: Your Challenge: Design a Tile Pattern
slides.storyContext: Now it's your turn. You have only a straightedge and compass.

example.problem: Can you construct a regular octagon (8-sided shape, each interior angle = 135°)? If yes, describe the steps. If no, explain why not using angle arithmetic.
example.solution: This is difficult with only compass and straightedge (unlike triangles and squares). A regular octagon requires special constructions involving angle trisection, which is NOT possible with compass and straightedge alone (a classical math fact). However, you CAN construct an octagon by cutting off the corners of a square: draw a square, then construct 45° angles at each corner (by bisecting 90°), and cut off the corners. This creates an octagon that tiles with squares.

slides.title: Timeless Beauty
slides.storyContext: Years later, travelers visit the village and marvel at the perfectly tiled stage. 'How did they make this without modern tools?' they ask. Anvi, now a young architect, smiles. 'With a straightedge, a compass, and the wisdom of geometry. The same techniques have been used for thousands of years.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Geometric constructions are timeless—the same methods used in ancient times still create perfect shapes today.

slides.title: Nature's Tilings: Hidden Patterns

points.text: Honeycombs use hexagonal tilings—the most efficient way to store honey and protect the colony.
Turtle shells and pinecones show triangular and spiral tilings found in nature.
Dragonfly wings and butterfly patterns often reflect geometric tessellations.

slides.inSimpleWords: Nature discovered tiling millions of years before humans—bees, tortoises, and insects all use perfect geometric patterns.

points.text: Geometric constructions use only straightedge and compass—no numbers needed—to create shapes with exact relationships.
Key constructions: equilateral triangles, squares, angle bisectors.
Tilings (tessellations) are patterns where shapes fit together with no gaps or overlaps.
The angles at any meeting point in a tiling must sum to exactly 360°.
Only three regular shapes tile perfectly: equilateral triangles, squares, and regular hexagons.
Real-world use: architects, tile makers, and bees use tilings for strength, beauty, and efficiency.

subject: Mathematics
title: Raj's Mystery Box: Solving Equations
hook: Help a clever shopkeeper solve real problems using equations—no guessing, just logic.

characters.name: Raj
characters.role: a village shopkeeper who uses math in daily business

characters.name: Karan
characters.role: a regular customer who brings tricky problems

slides.title: Finding the Unknown: Raj's Mystery Box
The Mystery Box
slides.storyContext: Raj's shop sells flour, rice, and spices in the marketplace. One day, Karan arrives with a puzzle: "Raj, I have a box. If I put 5 kilos of rice in it, and the total weight is 12 kilos, how heavy is the empty box?" Raj scratches his head. His daughter Priya says, "Dad, that's an equation! The unknown is the box's weight." Raj learns that algebra—finding the unknown—is just a smart way to solve real problems without guessing.

image.alt: The Mystery Box — Finding the Unknown

slides.title: What Is an Equation? What Is an Unknown?
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: "An equation is like a balanced scale, Dad. On one side, you have the box plus 5 kilos of rice. On the other side, the scale shows 12 kilos. They're equal."

points.label: Equation
points.text: A statement that two expressions are equal, using the symbol '='. Example: box + 5 = 12.

points.label: Unknown (or variable)
points.text: A quantity we don't know yet, usually written as a letter like x, y, or (in Raj's case) 'box'. Example: x + 5 = 12, where x is the weight of the box.

points.label: Solution
points.text: The value of the unknown that makes the equation true. In this case, box = 7 kilos, because 7 + 5 = 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: An equation is a math sentence that says two things are equal. The unknown is what we're looking for. To solve it, find the number that makes the equation true.

image.alt: What Is an Equation? What Is an Unknown? — Finding the Unknown

slides.title: Priya's Discovery
slides.storyContext: Priya starts playing with small weights and a scale at home. She puts 7 kilos on one side and writes 'x + 5' on a card for the other. 'See, Dad? If x is the box, then x + 5 equals 12. That's just saying what we already know, but in math language.' Raj nods. 'So algebra is just translating a problem into a balanced sentence, then solving it. Priya, you're a natural!'

slides.title: Simple Equations: The Box Problem
slides.storyContext: Let's solve Karan's original puzzle together.

example.problem: A box weighs some amount. Inside it, 5 kilos of rice. Total weight: 12 kilos. Find the weight of the empty box.
example.solution: Let x = weight of empty box. Equation: x + 5 = 12. Subtract 5 from both sides: x = 7 kilos. Check: 7 + 5 = 12. ✓

slides.title: Setting Up an Equation from Words
slides.storyContext: Karan brings more puzzles to the shop. "Raj, I bought some apples at 3 rupees each. I spent 60 rupees total. How many apples did I buy?" Priya says, "Let's translate that to an equation."

points.label: Step 1: Identify the unknown
points.text: Let x = the number of apples.

points.label: Step 2: Write the equation
points.text: Price per apple × number of apples = total spent. So: 3x = 60.

points.label: Step 3: Solve (find x)
points.text: Divide both sides by 3: x = 60 ÷ 3 = 20 apples.

example.problem: A shopkeeper has twice as many mangoes as guavas. If she has 30 guavas, write an equation and find the number of mangoes.
example.solution: Let x = number of mangoes. Equation: x = 2 × 30. Solution: x = 60 mangoes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Read the problem carefully. Find the unknown (what you're looking for). Translate words into an equation using + − × ÷. Then solve it.

slides.title: Apples at the Market
slides.storyContext: Priya watches as a customer in Raj's shop buys apples. 'I need 20 apples at 3 rupees each,' the customer says. Priya quickly calculates: '20 × 3 = 60 rupees.' The customer is amazed at her speed. 'That's the magic of equations, auntie,' Priya says with a smile.

slides.title: Multiplication Equations
slides.storyContext: Priya watches as a customer in Raj's shop buys bananas. 'I need 5 bananas and a bag. The total is 35 rupees. The bag costs 10 rupees. How much per banana?'

example.problem: If 5 bananas + 1 bag (10 rupees) = 35 rupees, find the price per banana.
example.solution: Let x = price per banana. Equation: 5x + 10 = 35. Subtract 10: 5x = 25. Divide by 5: x = 5 rupees per banana. Check: 5(5) + 10 = 35. ✓

slides.title: Solving Equations: The Balance Method
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches Raj the secret: "Think of an equation as a balance scale. Whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other to keep it balanced."

points.label: Principle
points.text: An equation stays equal if you add, subtract, multiply, or divide the SAME number on both sides.

points.label: Goal
points.text: Isolate the unknown on one side of the equation.

points.label: Example
points.text: Solve x + 7 = 15. Subtract 7 from both sides: (x + 7) − 7 = 15 − 7. Result: x = 8.

example.problem: Solve 3x = 24.
example.solution: Divide both sides by 3: 3x ÷ 3 = 24 ÷ 3. So x = 8. Check: 3 × 8 = 24. ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: A balance scale must stay balanced. If you add 5 to one side, add 5 to the other. If you take away half from one side, take away half from the other.

image.alt: Solving Equations: The Balance Method — Finding the Unknown

slides.title: The Scale That Breaks If You Cheat
slides.storyContext: Raj has an old balance scale in his shop that breaks if weights aren't balanced. 'That's what happens when an equation isn't balanced,' Priya says. 'If you add something to one side without adding to the other, the balance breaks. The equation is no longer true.'

slides.title: Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Priya solves x + 7 = 15 step by step for Karan to see.

slides.title: Find the Missing Weight
slides.storyContext: Priya sets up a scale game with her father. 'Dad, I put an unknown weight x on the left, and 15 on the right. The scale balances. Then I add 5 to the left and 5 to the right. Still balanced. What is x?'

example.problem: If x balances 15, and x + 5 balances 15 + 5, what is x?
example.solution: If x balances 15, then x = 15. Adding 5 to both sides: x + 5 = 20. This confirms x = 15.

slides.title: Equations with Unknowns on Both Sides
slides.storyContext: One day, Karan says: "Raj, I have a problem. I'm thinking of a number. If I add 5 to it, I get the same result as when I multiply it by 2. What's the number?" Priya sets it up: "Let x = the number. Then: x + 5 = 2x."

points.label: Strategy
points.text: Move all terms with the unknown to one side, and constants to the other.

points.label: Step 1
points.text: x + 5 = 2x. Subtract x from both sides: 5 = 2x − x = x.

example.problem: Solve 2y + 3 = y + 10.
example.solution: Subtract y from both sides: 2y − y + 3 = 10. So y + 3 = 10. Subtract 3 from both sides: y = 7. Check: 2(7) + 3 = 17, and 7 + 10 = 17. ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: If the unknown appears on both sides, move all unknowns to one side and numbers to the other. Keep the balance—whatever you do to one side, do to the other.

image.alt: Equations with Unknowns on Both Sides — Finding the Unknown

slides.title: Two Scales That Match
slides.storyContext: Priya imagines two scales side by side. 'If I have x + 5 on the left scale, and 2x on the right scale, and both are balanced, then they must be equal to each other. x + 5 = 2x. Now I just move things around to solve.'

slides.title: Solving Step by Step
slides.storyContext: Karan watches as Priya solves 3x − 2 = x + 6 on her slate. 'It looks messy at first, but if I move things one step at a time, it's easy.'

example.problem: Solve 3x − 2 = x + 6.
example.solution: Subtract x from both sides: 3x − x − 2 = 6. So 2x − 2 = 6. Add 2 to both sides: 2x = 8. Divide by 2: x = 4. Check: 3(4) − 2 = 10, and 4 + 6 = 10. ✓

slides.title: Real-World Equation: Raj's Grain Blend
slides.storyContext: Raj wants to blend two types of flour: regular flour at 20 rupees per kilo and premium flour at 40 rupees per kilo. He wants 10 kilos of a blend at 28 rupees per kilo average. How much of each flour should he use?

points.label: Set up
points.text: Let x = kilos of regular flour. Then (10 − x) = kilos of premium flour.

points.label: Cost equation
points.text: 20x + 40(10 − x) = 28 × 10. Cost of regular + cost of premium = total cost.

points.label: Solve
points.text: 20x + 400 − 40x = 280. Simplify: −20x = −120. So x = 6 kilos of regular flour, and 4 kilos of premium flour.

example.problem: Check Raj's answer: Is 6 kilos regular + 4 kilos premium = 10 kilos at 28 rupees per kilo average?
example.solution: Cost = 6(20) + 4(40) = 120 + 160 = 280 rupees. Average = 280 ÷ 10 = 28 rupees per kilo. ✓ It works!

slides.inSimpleWords: Many real problems have unknowns. Set up the equation carefully, translating the story. Solve step by step, keeping the balance.

slides.title: Mixing Spices: A Real Problem
slides.storyContext: A customer wants a spice blend. Cheap cumin costs 100 rupees per kilo, expensive cardamom costs 500 rupees per kilo. They want 2 kilos at 200 rupees per kilo average. Priya sets up the equation for her father. 'This is exactly like the flour blend, Dad, just different prices.'

slides.title: Solving the Spice Problem
slides.storyContext: Let x = kilos of cumin. Then (2 − x) = kilos of cardamom. Priya solves: 100x + 500(2 − x) = 200 × 2.

example.problem: Find how much cumin and cardamom for a 2-kilo blend at 200 rupees per kilo average.

slides.title: Checking Your Solution
slides.storyContext: Priya reminds Raj: "Always check your answer by plugging it back into the original equation. If it works, you're done. If not, you made a mistake somewhere."

points.label: Why check?
points.text: It catches arithmetic errors and confirms the solution is correct.

points.label: How
points.text: Substitute the solution back into the original equation. If both sides are equal, the solution is right.

points.label: Example
points.text: Original: x + 5 = 12. Solution: x = 7. Check: 7 + 5 = 12. ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: After solving, always plug your answer back into the original equation to check. Both sides should equal.

slides.title: The Time Raj Made a Mistake
slides.storyContext: Raj tries solving an equation in his head and gets 12. He plugs 12 back in and realizes it doesn't work. 'Oops!' he says. 'Good thing I checked, or I'd have given the wrong answer to a customer.' Priya smiles. 'That's why we always verify, Dad.'

slides.title: Raj's Customer Problem
slides.storyContext: Karan buys notebooks from Raj. Notebooks cost 15 rupees each. Karan has a 50-rupee note and gets 20 rupees back in change. How many notebooks did he buy?

example.problem: Set up and solve the equation.
example.solution: Let x = number of notebooks. Equation: 15x + 20 = 50 (notebooks cost plus change equals the note). Rearrange: 15x = 30. Divide: x = 2 notebooks. Check: 2 × 15 = 30, and 30 + 20 = 50. ✓

slides.title: Your Challenge: Solve the Riddle
slides.storyContext: Karan gives you one final puzzle: "I have a mystery number. If I subtract 8 and then multiply the result by 3, I get 21. What is my mystery number?"

example.problem: Set up and solve the equation to find Karan's mystery number.
example.solution: Let x = the mystery number. Equation: 3(x − 8) = 21. Divide both sides by 3: x − 8 = 7. Add 8 to both sides: x = 15. Check: 3(15 − 8) = 3(7) = 21. ✓ The mystery number is 15.

image.alt: Your Challenge: Solve the Riddle — Finding the Unknown

slides.title: Challenge: Solve These Equations
slides.storyContext: Karan leaves two more puzzles for you to solve.

slides.title: Challenge 1 and 2
slides.storyContext: Try solving both of these equations using the balance method.

slides.title: Priya's Own Riddle
slides.storyContext: That evening, Priya writes down her own equation: 5x + 2 = 3x + 8. She asks Karan, 'Can you solve this?' Karan works through it: Subtract 3x: 2x + 2 = 8. Subtract 2: 2x = 6. Divide by 2: x = 3. He checks: 5(3) + 2 = 17, and 3(3) + 8 = 17. ✓ 'Excellent!' Priya claps.

points.text: An equation is a balanced statement of two equal expressions. An unknown (variable) is what we solve for.
To solve an equation, isolate the unknown using the balance method: whatever you do to one side, do to the other.
Translate word problems into equations by identifying the unknown and expressing relationships mathematically.
Equations with unknowns on both sides: move all unknowns to one side and constants to the other.
Real-world problems (shopping, mixing, sharing) all use equations. Algebra is just organized thinking.
Always check your solution by substituting it back into the original equation.

image.alt: What You Learned — Finding the Unknown

subject: Science
title: Arjun's Journey: How Life Travels Through Bodies
hook: A village boy discovers why his heartbeat matters and how a plant drinks water.

slides.title: A Strange Discovery in the Garden
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Asha are helping water the tomato plants in Asha's farm when Dr. Malik visits. He asks: 'Do you know how water reaches the top leaves of a 2-meter plant? It doesn't have a pump.' Arjun realizes he's never thought about how plants 'drink.'

slides.title: What Is Transportation?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Transportation is the movement of substances (water, nutrients, oxygen) from one part of an organism to another.

points.label: Why needed
points.text: Plants need water and minerals from roots to leaves. Animals need oxygen in blood and nutrients to all cells.

points.label: Two systems
points.text: Animals have circulatory systems; plants have vascular systems.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every living thing needs a delivery system to move water, food, and air to where they're needed.

slides.title: Arjun Feels His Pulse
slides.storyContext: Dr. Malik places Arjun's finger on his own neck. 'Feel that? That's your heartbeat. About 70 times per minute. Each beat is your heart pushing blood throughout your entire body. Without it, every cell starves.' Arjun's eyes widen. 'So my heart is like a pump?'

slides.title: The Heart: The Body's Pump

points.label: What it is
points.text: A muscular organ about the size of a fist, located slightly left of center in the chest.

points.label: What it does
points.text: Pumps blood to the entire body about 70–80 times per minute (your pulse).

points.label: Four chambers
points.text: Right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle. Blood flows one way through valves.

slides.inSimpleWords: Your heart is like a pump that pushes blood through tubes (blood vessels) all over your body.

image.alt: The Heart: The Body's Pump — Transportation in Animals and Plants

slides.title: Arjun's Heartbeat Count
slides.storyContext: Dr. Malik teaches Arjun to count his pulse. 'Put your finger on your neck. Count the beats for 15 seconds, then multiply by 4. That's your resting heart rate.'

slides.title: Racing Hearts
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Asha run around the farm. Their hearts beat much faster now. 'Look at me now—100 beats per minute!' Arjun says breathlessly. Dr. Malik explains: 'When your muscles work hard, they need more oxygen. Your heart pumps faster to deliver it.'

slides.title: Which Type of Vessel Carries What?
slides.storyContext: Dr. Malik quizzes the children on the three types of blood vessels.

slides.title: White Blood Cells: The Defenders
slides.storyContext: Dr. Malik draws tiny knights on the sand. 'White blood cells patrol your blood like knights guarding a castle. When germs try to invade, these knights attack and destroy them.'

slides.title: How Platelets Stop Bleeding
slides.storyContext: Arjun gets a small cut. Asha watches as the blood stops flowing after a few seconds. 'How does that happen so fast?' Dr. Malik smiles. 'Platelets race to the cut and plug it up, like a team of construction workers sealing a leak.'

slides.title: Blood Vessels: The Highway System
slides.storyContext: Dr. Malik draws a diagram in the sand. 'Picture a city with roads leaving the central pump (the heart) going outward. Those are arteries. Then roads coming back from the city are veins. And everywhere in the city, tiny capillary streets let blood talk to the cells.'

slides.title: Blood Vessels: The Delivery Network

points.label: Arteries
points.text: Carry oxygen-rich blood AWAY from the heart. Thick walls, high pressure.

points.label: Veins
points.text: Carry oxygen-poor blood BACK to the heart. Thin walls, low pressure, have one-way valves.

points.label: Capillaries
points.text: Microscopic vessels where oxygen and nutrients exchange with cells. Thin walls allow diffusion.

example.problem: A student cuts their arm and sees bright red blood spurting. Is it from an artery or vein?
example.solution: Bright red blood that spurts rhythmically = artery (oxygen-rich, high pressure). Dark blood trickling = vein.

slides.inSimpleWords: Arteries push blood out; veins pull it back; capillaries let oxygen jump to your cells.

slides.title: Why Veins Look Blue
slides.storyContext: Asha asks, 'Why are veins blue but arteries are red?' Dr. Malik explains: 'Arteries carry oxygen-rich blood (bright red). Veins carry blood returning to the lungs, with less oxygen (dark red). Under the skin, that dark red looks bluish. The blood is still inside your body!'

slides.title: What Does Blood Carry?

points.label: Red blood cells
points.text: Carry oxygen from lungs to cells. Make blood red.

points.label: White blood cells
points.text: Fight infections and germs.

points.label: Platelets
points.text: Help blood clot when you get a cut.

points.label: Plasma
points.text: Liquid part carries nutrients, hormones, and waste.

slides.inSimpleWords: Blood is a superhighway carrying oxygen, food, and cleanup crews.

slides.title: Why Plants Droop Without Water
slides.storyContext: Asha watches a plant wilting after skipping water for two days. 'Look, Arjun. No water means no transport of nutrients. The plant can't carry food from leaves to roots. And no water to keep cells firm. It droops.' She waters it and within hours, it perks up again.

slides.title: Plants Don't Have Hearts—But They Do Have Pipes

points.label: Xylem
points.text: Tubes carrying water and minerals UP from roots to leaves. Like tiny straws.

points.label: Phloem
points.text: Tubes carrying sugar (made in leaves) DOWN to all parts of the plant.

points.label: Capillary action
points.text: Water climbs up xylem tubes against gravity because water molecules stick to the tube walls.

example.problem: Why does a cut flower in a vase stay fresh longer if you cut the stem again under water?
example.solution: A fresh cut removes blocked xylem tubes, so water can be pulled up again to keep petals firm.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants have two pipeline systems: one carries water up, one carries food down.

slides.title: Xylem Tubes Visible in Leaves
slides.storyContext: Priya looks at a leaf with a magnifying glass and traces the veins inside. 'These are xylem tubes!' she says. 'Water travels through them, and so do nutrients.'

slides.title: Phloem: The Food Highway
slides.storyContext: Grandpa explains to Arjun: 'Leaves make sugar using sunlight. That sugar travels down through phloem tubes to feed the roots and stems. It's like a delivery route—from the factory (leaves) to the warehouse (roots).'

slides.title: The Two-Way Traffic System in Plants

points.label: Xylem direction
points.text: Always goes UP, from roots to leaves. Water and minerals travel against gravity.

points.label: Phloem direction
points.text: Can go UP or DOWN. Sugar travels wherever the plant needs it most (roots, fruits, flowers).

points.label: Parallel pipes
points.text: Xylem and phloem tubes run side by side, forming the vascular bundle in stems and roots.

slides.inSimpleWords: Xylem is a one-way street going UP. Phloem is a two-way street—sugar goes wherever it's needed.

slides.title: Why Cut Flowers Droop
slides.storyContext: Arjun cuts a flower and forgets to put it in water. By evening, it droops. Asha places it in water, and by next morning, it's perky again. 'The water brings life back,' Asha says.

slides.title: The Mystery of Dyed Carnations
slides.storyContext: Asha puts a white carnation stem in red-colored water. After 2 hours, the white petals turn red. 'How is the color traveling?' she asks Dr. Malik. He smiles, 'That's xylem at work. The water (and dye) travel straight up.'

slides.title: The Mystery of Celery Stems
slides.storyContext: Asha puts a white carnation stem in red-colored water. After 2 hours, the white petals turn red. 'How is the color traveling?' she asks Dr. Malik.

points.label: What happens
points.text: The dye travels through xylem tubes just like water does.

points.label: How to see it
points.text: If you cut a stalk of celery lengthwise, you can see red dye lines—those are the xylem tubes.

example.problem: Explain how dyed water enters white flower petals.
example.solution: Water absorbed by roots travels up xylem tubes. Dye dissolves in water and rises with it, coloring the petals.

slides.title: Arjun's Experiment with Xylem
slides.storyContext: The next day, Arjun tries the celery experiment at home. He cuts a stalk, places it in red dye, and waits. By evening, red lines trace through the celery. 'Just like blood vessels in my arm!' he says, marveling at the parallel.

slides.title: Comparing Hearts and Roots
slides.storyContext: Dr. Malik draws two diagrams: a beating heart and a plant root absorbing water. 'Both are pumping systems,' he says. 'One pumps blood. One pumps water and minerals. The pump looks different, but the job is the same: move what's needed from one place to another.'

slides.title: Why Roots Absorb Water Constantly
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks, 'If plants don't have hearts, how do they pump water up against gravity?' Dr. Malik explains capillary action with a straw and water.

slides.title: What We Learned: The Flow of Life

points.text: Transportation moves water, nutrients, oxygen, and waste in living things.
Animals have hearts pumping blood through arteries, capillaries, and veins.
Blood carries oxygen, food, and defense cells to every part of the body.
Plants use xylem (water up) and phloem (food down) to distribute resources.
Capillary action helps plants overcome gravity—water climbs on its own.

slides.inSimpleWords: Life flows: hearts pump, blood carries, roots drink, and plants share food across their bodies.

subject: Science
title: The Mango Tree's Secret: How Plants Make Babies
hook: Why do mango trees flower in spring, and how does pollen travel from tree to tree?

image.alt: Reproduction in Plants — Reproduction in Plants

slides.title: The Mango Blossoms Arrive
slides.storyContext: Priya's grandfather's mango orchard explodes with white flowers every March. Priya asks: 'Why do flowers only come once a year? And how do these flowers become mangoes?' Grandpa smiles and invites her to watch the bees work.

slides.title: Sexual vs. Asexual Reproduction in Plants

points.label: Sexual reproduction
points.text: Uses flowers and seeds. Pollen (male) joins ovule (female) to create seeds with two parents' genes.

points.label: Asexual reproduction
points.text: One plant produces a copy (runners, bulbs, fragmentation). No seeds, identical offspring.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Sexual: mangoes, wheat, rice. Asexual: strawberry runners, potato buds, ginger rhizomes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants make babies two ways: with flowers and pollen (two parents), or by cloning themselves (one parent).

slides.title: Why One Strategy Is Not Enough
slides.storyContext: Grandpa explains: 'Mangoes use flowers and seeds—it takes time and needs bees. But ginger plants clone themselves underground and spread fast. Each strategy has pros and cons.'

slides.title: Grandpa's Lesson on Timing
slides.storyContext: Grandpa points to the calendar. 'Mangoes flower in spring—March and April—when the weather is warm and dry. Bees are active then. It's perfect timing. Evolution gave mango trees a clock that says, "Now is the time."'

slides.title: Flower Parts: The Reproductive Hardware

points.label: Sepal & Petal
points.text: Protect the flower and attract pollinators (bees, birds). Petals are colored.

points.label: Stamen (male)
points.text: Filament (stalk) topped with anther (pollen sacs). Produces pollen grains.

points.label: Carpel/Pistil (female)
points.text: Stigma (sticky tip), style (stalk), ovary (base). Contains ovules.

example.problem: Why are flower petals brightly colored and scented, but stamens and carpels are often hidden inside?
example.solution: Petals advertise to insects. Pollen and ovules are kept inside to stay dry and be precisely placed on pollinators.

slides.inSimpleWords: A flower is like a tiny factory: petals are the billboard, stamens make pollen, the carpel catches pollen.

image.alt: Flower Parts: The Reproductive Hardware — Reproduction in Plants

slides.title: Priya Watches the Bees
slides.storyContext: Priya lies in the grass, watching bees move from flower to flower. 'They're covered in yellow dust,' she notices. Grandpa says, 'That dust is pollen. The bees don't know they're delivering mail from male stamens to female carpels. Nature set up a beautiful trick.'

slides.title: Pollination: Pollen on the Move

points.label: Definition
points.text: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma (same flower or different flower).

points.label: Agents
points.text: Bees, butterflies, hummingbirds, wind, water. Many flowers evolved to match their pollinator.

points.label: Bee example
points.text: Bright flowers with nectar attract bees. Sticky pollen grains cling to bee's body. As bee visits next flower, pollen rubs onto stigma.

slides.inSimpleWords: Pollination is pollen hitchhiking on an insect's body or riding the wind to a new flower.

slides.title: Raj's Bees Do the Work
slides.storyContext: Raj, the beekeeper's son, is proud of his colony. 'My bees visit thousands of flowers. Every bee is a pollinator. One bee might visit 50 to 100 flowers in a single trip. That's how mangoes happen.'

slides.title: Dissecting a Flower: What's Inside?
slides.storyContext: Priya carefully pulls apart a mango flower petal by petal, and Grandpa labels each part: sepal, petal, stamen, carpel.

slides.title: Wind Pollination vs. Insect Pollination
slides.storyContext: Grandpa shows Priya two types of flowers: mango flowers (need bees) and grass flowers (blown by wind). 'Grass flowers are tiny and dull, no perfume. The wind doesn't care about pretty colors!'

slides.title: Types of Pollination

points.label: Insect pollination
points.text: Bright, scented flowers attract bees, butterflies, etc. Sticky pollen clings to their bodies.

points.label: Wind pollination
points.text: Lightweight, dry pollen floats on the breeze. Flowers are small and dull. No nectar needed.

points.label: Water pollination
points.text: Rare in flowering plants, but some aquatic plants use water currents to spread pollen.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different flowers have different mail carriers: bees, wind, or water.

slides.title: Why Mangoes Depend on Bees
slides.storyContext: Raj's bees are essential for the orchard. Without them, few flowers would become mangoes. Grandpa says, 'The orchard pays the bees in nectar. The bees pay us in mangoes.'

slides.title: The Flower's Secret Signal
slides.storyContext: Priya notices that some flowers are open in the morning and closed by afternoon. Grandpa explains: 'Flowers open when their pollinators are active. Sunflowers open for bees in the morning. Night-blooming flowers open for moths at dusk. It's all timed.' Priya marvels at the coordination.

slides.title: Fertilization: When Pollen Meets Ovule

points.label: Pollen tube
points.text: Pollen grain lands on stigma and grows a tube down through style into ovary.

points.label: Fusion
points.text: Male gamete (in pollen) fuses with female gamete (in ovule). Creates fertilized seed.

points.label: Double fertilization
points.text: In flowering plants, a second fusion creates endosperm (food for baby plant).

slides.inSimpleWords: The pollen's male cell dives down to meet the ovule's female cell. They fuse and create a seed.

slides.title: The Pollen Tube's Journey
slides.storyContext: Grandpa draws a picture in the sand. 'When pollen lands on the stigma, it's like a love letter arriving. But the letter must travel down the style into the ovary. That journey takes hours, sometimes days. The pollen grows a tiny tube and pushes its male cell down. Finally, fusion happens.'

slides.title: Why Flowers Need Different Pollinators
slides.storyContext: Priya notices that some flowers are tall and trumpet-shaped, others are small and flat. Grandpa explains: 'Different pollinators have different shapes. Hummingbird flowers are tube-shaped so the bird's long beak fits. Butterfly flowers are landing platforms. Each flower evolved to fit its pollinator perfectly.'

slides.title: From Flower to Fruit and Seed

points.label: Ovary becomes fruit
points.text: After fertilization, ovary walls thicken and ripen. Mango, apple, bean pod are all fruits.

points.label: Seed structure
points.text: Seed coat (protection), cotyledon (stored food), embryo (baby plant).

points.label: Dispersal
points.text: Seeds spread by wind (maple wings), water (coconut floats), animals (burs stick to fur), or water/wind.

example.problem: A seed inside a mango fruit has no way to move on its own. How does it travel to grow somewhere new?
example.solution: Animals eat the mango, digest fruit pulp, but the seed survives and is dropped far away in animal dung. Wind and water also carry lightweight seeds.

slides.inSimpleWords: The fruit protects and spreads seeds. Each seed is a tiny plant with a lunch box (cotyledon).

image.alt: From Flower to Fruit and Seed — Reproduction in Plants

slides.title: The Life of a Pollen Grain
slides.storyContext: Priya imagines she's a pollen grain. 'I'm made in the anther, sticky and yellow. A bee lands on a flower, I stick to her leg. She flies to the next flower, and I land on the stigma. Now I can grow down to the ovule!'

slides.title: Seeds vs. Bulbs vs. Runners
slides.storyContext: Grandpa shows Priya three ways plants reproduce: mango seeds (sexual), onion bulbs (asexual), and strawberry runners (asexual).

slides.title: From Seed to Seedling
slides.storyContext: Priya plants a mango seed. For weeks, nothing happens. Then one day, a tiny shoot breaks through the soil. 'It's waking up!' she says. 'The baby plant was waiting inside the seed coat all along.'

slides.title: The Mango's Journey Begins
slides.storyContext: After fertilization, Priya watches the tiny mango grow larger each week. 'It starts the size of a marble,' Grandpa says. 'By summer, it'll be as big as your fist. All that growth comes from the seed's energy and food reserves, plus the plant's photosynthesis.'

slides.title: How Many Seeds in a Mango?
slides.storyContext: Priya cuts open a ripe mango and counts the seeds inside. Just one large seed! Grandpa explains: 'One seed per fruit is enough. But a mango tree makes thousands of flowers. Even if only a few become mangoes, that's plenty to keep the tree alive.'

slides.title: Asexual Reproduction: Strawberries and Potatoes
slides.storyContext: Priya notices strawberry runners creeping across the garden. Each runner has a baby plant. Grandpa says: 'These babies are clones of the mother—exact copies. No pollen, no flowers needed.' Priya wonders: 'How is that possible?'

points.label: Vegetative reproduction
points.text: Plant stem or root produces a copy using mitosis (no mixing of genes).

points.label: Examples
points.text: Strawberry runners, potato tubers (with buds/eyes), ginger rhizomes, onion bulbs.

example.problem: Why are potatoes easier to grow than wheat?
example.solution: Potatoes grow from tuber eyes (asexual), so each eye clone grows a full plant. Wheat needs seeds (sexual), which require pollination and take longer.

slides.title: Why Farmers Love Asexual Plants
slides.storyContext: Priya's grandfather grows potatoes by planting small pieces of last year's potatoes. 'No guessing if they'll be good. Each piece grows an exact copy. Predictable, fast, reliable. But sexual reproduction—like mangoes—takes time and depends on bees. Different strategies for different plants.'

slides.title: Growing from Bulbs
slides.storyContext: Priya plants onion bulbs in the garden. Grandpa explains: 'A bulb is a mini plant packed with food. It already has a shoot inside. Just add water and soil, and it grows. No pollination needed. That's asexual reproduction.'

slides.title: The Cycle of Plant Life

points.text: Flowers are reproductive organs: stamens make pollen (male), carpels hold ovules (female).
Pollination moves pollen via bees, wind, water, or birds.
Fertilization fuses pollen with ovule, creating a seed inside a fruit.
Seeds germinate into new plants; fruits help disperse them.
Asexual reproduction (runners, tubers, bulbs) clones plants without flowers or pollen.

slides.inSimpleWords: Flowers make pollen, insects move it, ovules become seeds, fruits spread them, and some plants just copy themselves.

image.alt: The Cycle of Plant Life — Reproduction in Plants

subject: Science
title: The Cricket Match Clock: Understanding Speed and Time
hook: How fast is a ball traveling, and how do we measure motion?

image.alt: Motion and Time — Motion and Time

slides.title: The Fast Ball at the Match
slides.storyContext: During a village cricket match, a fast bowler releases the ball. It zooms past the batter in a blur. Coach Dev says: 'That's a 90 km/h ball.' Vikram asks: 'How do they know it's going 90 and not 80?' Sneha pulls out a notebook: 'It's about distance and time.'

image.alt: The Fast Ball at the Match — Motion and Time

slides.title: What Is Motion?

points.label: Definition
points.text: A change in position of an object relative to a reference point.

points.label: Reference point
points.text: An object or location we use to tell if something moved. A car moving at 60 km/h is fast relative to the ground but stationary relative to other cars on the highway.

points.label: Types
points.text: Uniform motion (same speed), non-uniform motion (changing speed).

slides.inSimpleWords: Motion is a change in where something is. Whether something moves depends on what you compare it to.

image.alt: What Is Motion? — Motion and Time

slides.title: Vikram Runs to the Store
slides.storyContext: Vikram decides to run to the store to buy supplies. He starts from home and runs 2 km toward the market. Then he realizes he forgot his wallet, so he runs 1 km back toward home. Finally, he gets the wallet and runs 2 km forward again to reach the market. Sneha watches and asks: 'How far did you actually travel, and how far are you from home?'

slides.title: Distance vs. Displacement

points.label: Distance
points.text: Total length of path traveled. Always positive. 'I walked 5 km around the village square.'

points.label: Displacement
points.text: Straight-line distance and direction from start to end. Can be zero if you return to start. 'I walked around the square and returned, displacement = 0 km.'

points.label: Example
points.text: Running 400 m on a circular track: distance = 400 m, displacement = 0 m.

example.problem: A delivery boy rides 3 km east to a house, then 4 km west back toward home. What is his distance and displacement?
example.solution: Distance = 3 + 4 = 7 km. Displacement = 3 − 4 = 1 km west.

slides.inSimpleWords: Distance is the full journey; displacement is the straight line from start to finish.

image.alt: Distance vs. Displacement — Motion and Time

slides.title: Vikram's Store Run Calculation
slides.storyContext: Let's calculate Vikram's actual journey.

example.problem: Vikram runs 2 km toward market, 1 km back home, then 2 km toward market again. What is total distance and final displacement?
example.solution: Distance = 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 km (add all segments). Displacement = 2 − 1 + 2 = 3 km from home toward market.

slides.title: Speed: How Fast Are You Going?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Speed = Total distance / Total time. Example: 100 km in 2 hours = 50 km/h.

points.label: Units
points.text: km/h (kilometers per hour), m/s (meters per second). To convert: 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h.

points.label: Average speed
points.text: Distance covered per unit time over a journey (may vary during journey).

points.label: Instantaneous speed
points.text: Speed at one exact moment (what a speedometer shows).

example.problem: A bus travels 240 km in 4 hours. What is its average speed?
example.solution: Speed = 240 km / 4 hours = 60 km/h.

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed tells you how much distance you cover per hour (or per second).

image.alt: Speed: How Fast Are You Going? — Motion and Time

slides.title: The Cricket Ball Speed Radar
slides.storyContext: At the cricket match, Coach Dev shows Vikram a radar gun. It measures how fast the ball travels. A ball bowled 22 meters (length of pitch) reaches the batter in 0.24 seconds. Coach Dev says: 'The faster the ball, the fewer seconds it takes. That's how we know speed.'

example.problem: A cricket ball travels 22 meters in 0.24 seconds. Convert to km/h.
example.solution: Speed = 22 m / 0.24 s = 91.67 m/s. Convert: 91.67 m/s × 3.6 = 330 km/h. (Note: this is unrealistic—actual bowling is ~30–35 m/s = 108–126 km/h, but math works the same way.)

slides.title: Velocity: Speed with Direction

points.label: Definition
points.text: Velocity = Displacement / Time, including direction. Example: '50 km/h north.'

points.label: Difference from speed
points.text: Speed is 'how fast'; velocity is 'how fast and which way.'

points.label: Example
points.text: Two cars: Car A: 60 km/h east. Car B: 60 km/h west. Same speed, opposite velocities.

slides.inSimpleWords: Velocity is speed plus direction. A GPS gives you velocity; a speedometer gives you speed.

image.alt: Velocity: Speed with Direction — Motion and Time

slides.title: The Direction Matters
slides.storyContext: Sneha explains to Vikram: 'Two runners on a circular track both run at 10 km/h, but one goes clockwise and one goes counterclockwise. Their speeds are the same, but their velocities are different—they're going in opposite directions.'

example.problem: Two cyclists ride on a straight road. Cyclist A travels 40 km north in 2 hours. Cyclist B travels 40 km south in 2 hours. Compare their speeds and velocities.
example.solution: Both have speed = 40 km / 2 hours = 20 km/h. But velocities: A = 20 km/h north, B = 20 km/h south. Same speed, opposite velocities.

slides.title: Acceleration: Speeding Up, Slowing Down, or Changing Direction

points.label: Definition
points.text: Change in velocity per unit time. Acceleration = (Final velocity − Initial velocity) / Time.

points.label: Types
points.text: Speeding up (positive), slowing down/deceleration (negative), changing direction (even at same speed).

points.label: Example
points.text: A car goes from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 seconds. Acceleration = 20 / 5 = 4 m/s².

example.problem: A cricket ball at rest is hit by a bat and reaches 30 m/s in 0.1 seconds. Find its acceleration.
example.solution: Acceleration = (30 m/s − 0 m/s) / 0.1 s = 300 m/s². (Very fast!)

slides.inSimpleWords: Acceleration is how quickly your speed or direction changes.

image.alt: Acceleration: Speeding Up, Slowing Down, or Changing Direction — Motion and Time

slides.title: Starting the Race
slides.storyContext: Vikram prepares for a 100-meter sprint. At the starting line, he accelerates from rest, reaching maximum speed midway through, then decelerates slightly at the end to avoid crashing into the finish line banner. Coach Dev watches with a stopwatch and notes how Vikram's speed changes throughout the race.

example.problem: Vikram runs a 100 m sprint. From 0–50 m, he accelerates from 0 to 10 m/s (50 m in 10 seconds). From 50–100 m, he maintains 10 m/s. What is his average acceleration in the first phase?
example.solution: Acceleration = (10 m/s − 0 m/s) / 10 s = 1 m/s². He speeds up at 1 meter per second every second.

slides.title: Understanding Non-Uniform Motion
slides.storyContext: Sneha explains: 'Not everything moves at the same speed. Vikram starts slow, speeds up, then tires out and slows down. That's non-uniform motion. The speedometer in a car changes constantly—that's why we have seatbelts for sudden acceleration and braking.'

slides.title: Uniform vs. Non-Uniform Motion

points.label: Uniform motion
points.text: Speed stays constant. A car on a highway at steady 60 km/h.

points.label: Non-uniform motion
points.text: Speed changes. A car accelerating, braking, or climbing a hill.

points.label: Real world
points.text: Most real motion is non-uniform. Uniform motion is rare and useful for calculations.

slides.inSimpleWords: Uniform = steady speed. Non-uniform = speed changing.

example.problem: A scooter travels 0–10 km at 20 km/h, then 10–30 km at 60 km/h. What is the average speed?
example.solution: First segment: 10 km at 20 km/h = 0.5 hours. Second segment: 20 km at 60 km/h = 0.33 hours. Total: 30 km in 0.83 hours = 36 km/h average.

slides.title: The Bus Journey
slides.storyContext: A local bus leaves at 8 AM to travel 60 km. It accelerates smoothly to 60 km/h in the first 10 minutes, maintains speed for 45 minutes, then brakes to a stop over 5 minutes. Sneha calculates whether this journey takes 1 hour.

points.label: Acceleration phase
points.text: 10 minutes at increasing speed averages ~30 km/h = 5 km.

points.label: Constant speed phase
points.text: 45 minutes at 60 km/h = 45 km.

points.label: Braking phase
points.text: 5 minutes from 60 km/h to 0 averages ~30 km/h = 2.5 km.

example.problem: Total distance = 5 + 45 + 2.5 = 52.5 km. With wait times at stops, does the journey take 1 hour?
example.solution: No. Just the motion takes ~1 hour. Add stops and it could be 1.5+ hours.

slides.title: Measuring Motion with Graphs
slides.storyContext: Coach Dev brings a distance-time graph to the next practice. He shows Vikram how a straight line means constant speed, while curves show acceleration or deceleration. 'The steeper the line, the faster you're going,' Coach says. Vikram realizes: 'So a flat line means I'm stopped!'

slides.title: Distance-Time Graphs

points.label: Horizontal line
points.text: Object is stationary (not moving).

points.label: Straight diagonal line
points.text: Constant speed. Steeper = faster.

points.label: Curve
points.text: Acceleration (speeding up or slowing down). Curves show non-uniform motion.

slides.inSimpleWords: On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means faster motion.

example.problem: A graph shows a straight line from (0, 0) to (2 hours, 100 km). What is the speed?
example.solution: Speed = 100 km / 2 hours = 50 km/h. The straight line indicates uniform motion.

slides.title: Motion Around Us
slides.storyContext: Sneha points out to Vikram: 'Look around. The wind is moving the leaves. Birds fly in curves—that's acceleration. The clouds drift slowly. The Sun moves across the sky. Even when you sleep, you're moving—Earth rotates!' Vikram laughs: 'Motion is everywhere!'

slides.title: Motion is Relative

points.label: Same object, different observers
points.text: A person sitting in a moving bus is at rest relative to the bus but moving relative to the ground.

points.label: Changing reference frame
points.text: Motion looks different from different viewpoints.

points.label: Why it matters
points.text: When we measure speed, we must always specify the reference (speed relative to what?).

slides.inSimpleWords: Motion is relative. Something can be still in one frame and moving in another.

example.problem: A person walks at 2 m/s inside a bus moving 20 m/s. What is their speed relative to the ground?
example.solution: If walking forward: 2 + 20 = 22 m/s. If walking backward: 20 − 2 = 18 m/s. Relative to the bus: 2 m/s always.

slides.title: The 400 m Race Analysis
slides.storyContext: Vikram runs a 400 m race on the school track in 1 minute (60 seconds). Sneha asks: 'What's your speed? Were you going the same speed the whole time?'

points.label: Average speed
points.text: 400 m / 60 s = 6.67 m/s or about 24 km/h.

points.label: Non-uniform motion
points.text: Vikram probably sprinted hard at the start, slowed midway, then pushed hard at the end.

example.problem: If Vikram ran the first 100 m in 12 seconds and the last 100 m in 16 seconds, did he accelerate or decelerate in the race?
example.solution: First 100 m speed = 100/12 = 8.33 m/s. Last 100 m = 100/16 = 6.25 m/s. He decelerated (slowed down) overall.

image.alt: The 400 m Race Analysis — Motion and Time

slides.title: Motion and Time Summary

points.text: Motion is change in position relative to a reference point.
Distance is total path; displacement is straight-line from start to end.
Speed = distance / time (scalar, no direction).
Velocity = displacement / time (vector, includes direction).
Acceleration is change in velocity over time (speeding, slowing, or direction change).
Uniform motion has constant speed; non-uniform motion has changing speed.

slides.inSimpleWords: Motion is measured by distance, speed, and time. Direction makes it velocity. Change means acceleration.

image.alt: Motion and Time Summary — Motion and Time

subject: Science
title: The Lightbulb Mystery: Current, Heat, and Magnets
hook: Why does a lightbulb get hot, and how does electricity make magnets?

image.alt: Electric Current and its Effects — Electric Current and its Effects

slides.title: Why Does the Bulb Glow?
slides.storyContext: During a power cut, Ravi uses a battery and flashlight. He wonders: 'Why does the filament glow when I switch it on? And why do nails stick to an electromagnet even when it's not a permanent magnet?' Divya invites him to her science club to find out.

slides.title: What Is Electric Current?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Flow of electric charge (usually electrons) through a conductor. Measured in amperes (A).

points.label: Conductor vs. insulator
points.text: Conductor: allows current to flow easily (copper, aluminum, water). Insulator: blocks current (rubber, plastic, glass).

points.label: Circuit needed
points.text: Current flows in a closed loop (circuit) from positive terminal of battery, through devices, back to negative terminal.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electric current is like water flowing through pipes—it needs a closed path to move.

image.alt: What Is Electric Current? — Electric Current and its Effects

slides.title: Ravi's First Experiment
slides.storyContext: Ravi connects a battery, wire, and bulb. Light! Then he tries breaking the wire—light goes out. He reconnects it—light returns. 'It's like a closed door—current can't get through if the door is open,' Mr. Kapoor explains. Ravi asks: 'What if I use two bulbs? Do they both light up equally?'

slides.title: Series vs. Parallel Circuits

points.label: Series
points.text: Bulbs/devices connected one after another in a single loop. If one bulb breaks, current stops and all go dark.

points.label: Parallel
points.text: Bulbs/devices connected on separate branches. Each gets full voltage. If one bulb breaks, others stay lit.

points.label: Home example
points.text: House lights are in parallel (each can switch on/off independently). Car lights were once series; now mostly parallel.

example.problem: Two bulbs in series powered by one battery. Brightness compared to one bulb alone?
example.solution: Each bulb gets half the voltage, so each is dimmer. Parallel: each bulb gets full voltage, so same brightness as one bulb alone.

slides.inSimpleWords: Series = one path (if one breaks, all stop). Parallel = many paths (one can break, others work).

example.problem: Three identical bulbs (each 3 V, 1 A) are connected to a 3 V battery. Compare brightness: (a) all series, (b) all parallel.
example.solution: (a) Series: each gets 1 V, dim. (b) Parallel: each gets 3 V, bright. Series bulbs are dim; parallel bulbs are bright.

slides.title: Design a Circuit for a Classroom
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor asks: 'How would you wire 10 lights in a classroom so each can switch on/off independently, and a burned-out bulb doesn't darken the whole room?' Ravi immediately knows: 'Parallel!'

slides.title: Thermal Effect of Current: Heat and Light

points.label: Joule heating
points.text: When current flows through a resistor, friction between moving electrons and atoms generates heat. Heat = I²Rt (Joule's law).

points.label: Incandescent bulb
points.text: Tungsten filament resists current heavily, gets red-hot (~2700 K), glows white. 95% energy wasted as heat.

points.label: Fuses and circuit breakers
points.text: Melt or trip when excessive current (short circuit) threatens to overheat wires and start fires.

slides.inSimpleWords: Current pushing through resistance creates heat and light. A thinner wire or tighter coil gets hotter faster.

image.alt: Thermal Effect of Current: Heat and Light — Electric Current and its Effects

slides.title: Why Does the Bulb Get Hot?
slides.storyContext: Divya holds a bulb (turned on) and pulls her hand back. 'Hot!' she says. Mr. Kapoor explains: 'The filament has high resistance. Current fighting through it heats it to ~2700 Kelvin. At that temperature, it glows white, and you feel the heat radiating.' Ravi asks: 'Why don't the wires connecting the battery get as hot?' 'Because they have low resistance,' Mr. Kapoor says. 'Most heat is generated where resistance is highest.'

example.problem: A bulb filament with resistance 100 Ω carries 0.5 A for 10 seconds. How much heat is generated? (Heat = I²Rt)

slides.title: Magnetic Effect of Current: Electromagnets

points.label: Magnetic field
points.text: Electric current flowing through a wire creates a magnetic field around it. Coil the wire and field strengthens.

points.label: Electromagnet
points.text: Wire coil around iron core + current = temporary magnet. Turn off current, magnetism stops.

points.label: Strength depends on
points.text: Current strength, number of coil turns, iron core presence.

example.problem: Why does wrapping wire around a nail multiple times make a stronger electromagnet than a single loop?
example.solution: More loops = magnetic field from each loop adds together. Iron core amplifies the combined field. Nail becomes temporary magnet.

slides.inSimpleWords: Coil a wire around a nail and run current through—the nail becomes a magnet as long as current flows.

slides.title: Ravi's Electromagnet
slides.storyContext: In the science club, Ravi wraps copper wire around a nail 20 times and connects it to a battery. 'Now touch it to paper clips,' Divya instructs. Ravi holds the electromagnet over paper clips and they jump up! He switches off the battery—the clips fall. 'It's magnetic, but only when current flows!' Ravi marvels. Mr. Kapoor nods: 'That's the difference from a permanent magnet. An electromagnet can be turned on and off.'

example.problem: An electromagnet with 50 coil turns around an iron nail picks up 30 paper clips. If you add another 50 turns (100 total), how many clips could it pick up (assuming current stays same)?
example.solution: Roughly double (to ~60 clips), because twice as many loops mean stronger combined field. Actual number depends on current and iron core saturation.

slides.title: Applications of Electromagnets

points.label: Electric bell
points.text: Electromagnet attracts a hammer, hammer strikes a bell, circuit breaks, electromagnet releases, spring returns hammer.

points.label: Relay
points.text: Small electromagnet controlled by switch opens/closes a separate high-power circuit.

points.label: Electric motor
points.text: Electromagnet in a magnetic field rotates, spinning an axle. Powers fans, drills, pumps.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electromagnets lift, ring, switch, and spin. No permanent magnet needed—just current.

image.alt: Applications of Electromagnets — Electric Current and its Effects

slides.title: The Electric Bell
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor shows a doorbell to the class. 'Press the button,' he says. When Ravi presses it, a hammer hits the bell—ding! 'That electromagnet pulls the hammer forward. But when it does, the circuit breaks, electromagnet releases, spring pushes hammer back, circuit reconnects, and the cycle repeats—ding, ding, ding!' Divya asks: 'So it rings continuously as long as I hold the button?' 'Exactly.'

slides.title: Real-World Electromagnets
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor takes students through the school. 'See the electric motor in the fan? Electromagnet. The relay in the circuit breaker? Electromagnet. The junkyard crane lifting scrap metal? Huge electromagnet.' Ravi realizes: 'Electromagnets are everywhere!'

slides.title: How an Electric Motor Works

points.label: Rotating coil
points.text: Electromagnet coil in a permanent magnetic field experiences forces that make it spin.

points.label: Commutator
points.text: Split ring that reverses current direction every half-rotation to keep coil spinning.

points.label: Speed control
points.text: More current = stronger rotation. More voltage = faster spin.

slides.inSimpleWords: A motor is an electromagnet spinning inside a permanent magnet's field.

slides.title: Design Your Own Electromagnet
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor challenges Ravi and Divya: 'Build an electromagnet that can lift 10 paper clips from a desk. You have copper wire, a nail, and a 1.5 V battery. What changes will make it stronger?'

points.label: Variables
points.text: Wire coil tightness, number of loops, battery voltage (use 2 batteries in series for 3 V), wire gauge (thickness).

points.label: Test method
points.text: Count paper clips lifted. More is better.

example.problem: Why does using 2 batteries (3 V) instead of 1 (1.5 V) make the electromagnet stronger?
example.solution: Higher voltage = more current through the coil = stronger magnetic field. The coil experiences more force.

slides.title: Resistance and Heating
slides.storyContext: Divya holds thick copper wire and thin nichrome wire, both connected to a battery. The thick wire stays cool; the thin wire glows red-hot. 'Thinner wire = higher resistance = more heat!' Mr. Kapoor explains. This is why toasters and heaters use thin wire.

slides.title: Resistance and Heat Generation

points.label: Resistance
points.text: Opposition to current flow. Thick wires: low resistance, cool. Thin wires: high resistance, hot.

points.label: Joule's law
points.text: Heat = I²Rt. More current, higher resistance, or longer time = more heat.

points.label: Practical uses
points.text: Toasters, heaters, electric ovens all use high-resistance wire to generate heat.

slides.inSimpleWords: Thin, high-resistance wire gets hotter than thick, low-resistance wire when the same current passes through.

slides.title: Current Matters in Electromagnets
slides.storyContext: Ravi builds two identical electromagnets but connects one to a fresh 1.5 V battery and another to an old, weak battery. The fresh battery electromagnet lifts 20 paper clips; the weak one lifts only 3. 'It's all about current!' Mr. Kapoor says. 'More current = stronger field.'

example.problem: Two electromagnets with 100 coil turns each: one with 0.5 A current, one with 1 A. How many times stronger is the second?
example.solution: Magnetic field strength is proportional to current. 1 A vs. 0.5 A = 2 times stronger. The second electromagnet can lift twice as many paper clips.

slides.title: Uses of Electromagnets in Daily Life

points.label: Doorbells and buzzers
points.text: Ring or buzz repeatedly when button held.

points.label: Microphones and speakers
points.text: Convert sound to current and back using electromagnets.

points.label: Magnetic locks
points.text: Hold doors shut with electromagnet; release when current cuts.

points.label: MRI machines
points.text: Powerful electromagnets create fields to image the human body.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electromagnets are used in almost every electrical device you touch.

slides.title: Safety with Electricity
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor shows the class a burned-out fuse. 'This saved a house from fire. When too much current flows (short circuit), the fuse melts and breaks the circuit before wires overheat and catch fire.' Ravi asks: 'How does the fuse know when there's too much current?' 'It melts when heat reaches a certain temperature,' Mr. Kapoor explains.

slides.title: Circuit Breakers and Safety

points.label: Fuse
points.text: Metal alloy that melts at high temperature, breaking circuit if current exceeds safe limit.

points.label: Circuit breaker
points.text: Automatic switch that trips (opens) when current exceeds safe level, preventing fire.

points.label: Earth/ground wire
points.text: Safety wire that carries excess current harmlessly into the ground if insulation fails.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fuses and circuit breakers protect you and your home from electrical fires.

slides.title: Electric Current and Its Effects

points.text: Electric current is flow of electrons through a closed circuit.
Series circuits share current (dim bulbs); parallel circuits share voltage (bright bulbs).
Current through resistance generates heat (Joule heating) and light (incandescent bulbs).
Current through a coil creates a magnetic field; coiled current is an electromagnet.
Electromagnets power bells, motors, relays, and many household devices.
Electromagnets turn on/off with current; permanent magnets cannot.

slides.inSimpleWords: Current heats and lights; coiled current creates magnets. No moving parts, just flowing electrons.

subject: Science
title: Aisha's Mirror Mystery: How Light Travels and Bounces
hook: Why do mirrors flip images, and why does a straw look bent in water?

image.alt: Light — Light

slides.title: The Straight Shadow
slides.storyContext: During an afternoon study session, Aisha holds a pencil in front of a lamp. The shadow on the wall is sharp and straight. She tilts the pencil—the shadow changes shape. Karan jokes: 'Light always travels in straight lines.' Aisha then puts a glass of water on the lamp and sees a straw inside look bent. 'That breaks your rule!' she says with a smile.

image.alt: The Straight Shadow — Light

slides.title: Light: What Is It?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Electromagnetic radiation that human eyes can see (wavelength 400–700 nanometers).

points.label: Source
points.text: Anything hot (Sun, flame, bulb filament) or fluorescent (glow stick, firefly).

points.label: Speed
points.text: Light travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s (300,000 km/s) in vacuum. Fastest thing known.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light is a wave of energy that travels in straight lines until it hits something.

image.alt: Light: What Is It? — Light

slides.title: The Speed of Light
slides.storyContext: Karan tells Aisha: 'Light travels so fast—300,000 km every single second. The light from the Sun takes 8 minutes to reach us. Light from the farthest stars takes years.' Aisha gasps: 'So I'm seeing the Sun as it was 8 minutes ago?'

slides.title: Rectilinear Propagation: Light Travels Straight

points.label: Definition
points.text: Light travels in straight lines in a uniform medium (same density).

points.label: Proof
points.text: Shadows are sharp-edged (not fuzzy). Pinhole camera creates inverted image. Laser beams are straight.

points.label: Exception
points.text: Light bends when entering a different medium (water, glass) due to change in speed.

example.problem: Why is the shadow of a pencil sharp on a wall close by but blurry on a wall far away during sunset?
example.solution: The Sun is a large source. Close wall: shadow edge sharp (blockage region small). Far wall: penumbra (partial shadow) grows large, so edge appears blurry.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light goes straight unless something stops it or it enters a new medium.

image.alt: Rectilinear Propagation: Light Travels Straight — Light

example.problem: A pinhole camera has a hole 1 cm in diameter. An object is 50 cm from the hole. Why does the image on the screen (50 cm behind hole) appear inverted?
example.solution: Light rays travel straight. Rays from the top of the object pass through the hole and hit the lower part of the screen. Rays from the bottom hit the top. This crossing inverts the image.

slides.title: Reflection: Light Bounces Off Mirrors

points.label: Law of reflection
points.text: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (measured from the normal, a line perpendicular to the surface).

points.label: Plane mirror
points.text: Flat mirror creates a virtual image same size as object, same distance behind mirror, laterally inverted.

points.label: Curved mirrors
points.text: Concave mirrors focus light (used in telescopes). Convex mirrors spread light (used in car side mirrors).

example.problem: A person standing 2 meters from a plane mirror sees their image. How far behind the mirror does the image appear?
example.solution: Virtual image appears 2 meters behind the mirror (same distance as object is in front).

slides.inSimpleWords: Mirrors bounce light at the same angle it arrives. Your mirror image is behind the mirror, same distance as you are in front.

image.alt: Reflection: Light Bounces Off Mirrors — Light

slides.title: The Mirror Trick
slides.storyContext: Aisha looks in a mirror and waves. Her reflection waves back, same timing. She holds up a book and the reflection holds up a reversed book. Teacher Neha explains: 'The mirror isn't reversing left-right. It's reversing front-back. Your right hand looks like the reflection's left because we're looking at the back of the reflection.'

example.problem: Aisha stands 1.5 meters in front of a plane mirror. She walks 0.5 meters closer. How far is she from her image now?
example.solution: New distance from mirror = 1.5 − 0.5 = 1 meter. Image is 1 meter behind mirror. Total distance from Aisha to image = 1 + 1 = 2 meters.

slides.title: Curved Mirrors: Concave and Convex

points.label: Concave mirror (curved inward)
points.text: Converges light to focal point. Magnifies close objects. Used in telescopes, makeup mirrors.

points.label: Convex mirror (curved outward)
points.text: Diverges light, spreads it apart. Shows wider field of view. Used as car side mirrors, security mirrors.

points.label: Focal point
points.text: Point where reflected light rays meet (concave) or appear to come from (convex).

slides.inSimpleWords: Concave mirrors converge light and magnify. Convex mirrors spread light and show more area.

slides.title: The Magnifying Mirror
slides.storyContext: Aisha finds a makeup mirror and discovers her face appears magnified—but only when she's close. When she moves far, the image inverts and shrinks. Teacher Neha explains: 'That's a concave mirror. Its focus point controls the image size and direction.'

slides.title: Refraction: Light Bends in Water

points.label: Definition
points.text: Light bends when passing from one medium to another due to change in speed.

points.label: Rule
points.text: Light slows in denser media (water, glass), causing bend toward the normal. Light speeds up leaving denser media, bend away from normal.

points.label: Real vs. apparent
points.text: Straw in water appears bent. Fish underwater appear shallower than they are. This is refraction.

example.problem: Why does a fish in water appear at a different depth than it really is?
example.solution: Light from the fish bends upward as it leaves water (less dense → more dense, it bends toward normal). Our eye traces the ray backwards, placing the fish higher than reality.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light bends when it enters water because it slows down. This makes things underwater look closer than they really are.

image.alt: Refraction: Light Bends in Water — Light

slides.title: The Bent Straw
slides.storyContext: Aisha fills a glass with water and puts a straw in it. Looking from the side, the straw looks bent at the water surface! Karan says: 'But the straw isn't really bent—the light is.' Aisha asks: 'Why?' Teacher Neha explains: 'Light travels slower in water than in air. When light bends from air to water, it changes direction. That makes the straw appear bent where air meets water.'

example.problem: Light from the straw's submerged part travels up through water to Aisha's eye. Does it bend away from or toward the normal (vertical line)?
example.solution: Light travels slower in water (denser), so it bends toward the normal as it enters water from air, and away from the normal as it exits. Since we see light exiting water, it bends away from normal, making the straw appear higher than it really is.

slides.title: Lenses: Curved Glass Focuses Light

points.label: Converging lens (convex)
points.text: Thicker in middle, thinner at edges. Bends light rays toward a focal point. Used in magnifying glasses, cameras, microscopes.

points.label: Diverging lens (concave)
points.text: Thinner in middle, thicker at edges. Spreads light rays outward. Used in peepholes, to correct near-sightedness.

points.label: Focal length
points.text: Distance from lens to focal point. Shorter focal length = stronger magnification.

slides.inSimpleWords: A convex lens brings light together (magnifies or focuses). A concave lens spreads light apart.

image.alt: Lenses: Curved Glass Focuses Light — Light

slides.title: The Magnifying Glass
slides.storyContext: Karan brings a magnifying glass to show Aisha how it magnifies small print. When she moves the glass closer to the paper, the text appears larger and sharper. When she moves too far away, the image disappears. 'There's a sweet spot,' Teacher Neha explains. 'That's the focal point of the lens.'

example.problem: A converging lens has focal length 5 cm. An object 10 cm from the lens creates an image. Is the image real or virtual, and how many times magnified?
example.solution: Object at 2× focal length creates a real, inverted image at 2× focal length on the other side. Magnification = 1× (same size). This is used in copy machines.

slides.title: The Candle and the Lens Experiment
slides.storyContext: Teacher Neha brings a convex lens and a candle. She places the lens between candle and wall, adjusts distance. A real, inverted image of the candle appears on the wall. Aisha asks: 'How is the image upside-down? And how is it bright without electricity?'

points.label: Real image
points.text: Light rays actually converge at a point on screen. Upside-down (inverted) because light rays cross at focal point.

points.label: Virtual image
points.text: Rays don't converge; eye traces rays backward (mirror, magnifying glass). Same way up as object.

example.problem: Using a convex lens, object at 2× focal length creates an image. Where and how large?
example.solution: Image appears at 2× focal length on opposite side, inverted, same size as object. Used in copy machines and projectors.

image.alt: The Candle and the Lens Experiment — Light

slides.title: Applications of Lenses
slides.storyContext: Karan shows Aisha his telescope and camera. 'Lenses in both,' he says. 'Telescope focuses distant starlight to my eye. Camera focuses sunlight onto film to capture images.' Teacher Neha adds: 'Glasses correct vision by using lenses to refocus light on your retina. Microscopes magnify tiny objects using multiple lenses together.'

slides.title: Real vs. Virtual Images

points.label: Real image
points.text: Light rays converge at actual point (screen can show it). Inverted. Example: projector, camera.

points.label: Virtual image
points.text: Light rays don't converge; eye traces them backward to a point. Upright. Example: mirror, magnifying glass.

points.label: When it matters
points.text: Real images can be displayed on screens. Virtual images can only be seen by looking through the lens.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real images appear on screens (inverted). Virtual images appear behind mirrors or in lenses (upright).

slides.title: Correcting Vision with Lenses
